utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic and Eugene O'Sullivan appearing for the Stanisic Defence this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Miroslav Cuskic for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And unless there is some reason to delay, could we have the witness back on the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Brown. Before I invite Mr. Krgovic to continue, I give the usual reminder, that you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You may remember that yesterday we discussed that document, Zupljanin's speech, or presentation, when he complains about the conduct of the army. I'll continue in the same vein. Do you know that the individual operations groups or groups or brigades placed the headquarters of their respective brigades in the police stations? In your paragraph 2.101 you mention such a group of brigades and you cite some documents of this type. The relevant footnote is 455. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to look at the reference, but I do know that in some cases the -- the police headquarters was used and I think the reference you're talking about is maybe to do with Skender Vakuf. But I'd have to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you document 2D07-0052 in -- under tab 8 in the Zupljanin Defence binder. Let me repeat, 2D07-0052. Mr. Brown, this is an order dated 16 July, as far as I can tell, by the Brigade Group Command Skender Vakuf. Let us see the signature on the last page. Actually, I think it's the last-but-one page. You see here as the commander of that brigade group Lieutenant-Colonel Bosko Peulic, and you see who it was sent to, the corps command, and the command of the 122nd Light Infantry Brigade. The command of the 1st Infantry Brigade and the command of the Light Kotor Varos Infantry Brigade. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it would seem to be that's the distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And I take it that you know that at the corps -- corps brigade --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction at the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Brigade groups were established to carry out tasks. In the general area of Vlasic this group was formed which was headed By Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I think Vlasic was a key tactical feature and was on the front line between Central Bosnia and the corps, and although Commander Peulic was concurrently commander of the 122nd Light Brigade he was also operations group commander, which had a wider zone, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As commander of that group, the Kotor Varos Light Brigade was subordinate to him and he was in a position to issue orders to them; correct?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that was the case, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please take a look at page 7 in the Serbian now. It's page 4 in the English version of this document. Item 5.3 the last paragraph reads: "The command post" - KM - "is to be located in the Kotor Varos SJB building and the forward command post" - IKM - "is to be set up on Mount Borja and at Krusevo Brdo village, as necessary." Did you have in mind this particular paragraph when in your report, you referred to the Kotor Varos Light Infantry Brigade?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I don't think my reference refers to this document or does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does? Okay. Yes, I guess that's what I mean. I know -- I think there were maybe other references, maybe in Skender Vakuf itself there was times they used the police station. But here it would seem to say that the command post of the Kotor Varos brigade is to be located in the police stations. And bearing in mind, I think the references in that 5.3 about cooperating with the SJB it wouldn't surprise me that was a -- that was to occur and I'm assuming the forward command post was to be placed in a location reasonably close to where they expected some activity to come, that would be usually what happened. And invariably the commander would at the forward command post and the rest of his staff would be at the command post itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The headquarter of this brigade group and of Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic was at Skender Vakuf, isn't that what you wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right, yes, sir. I don't know the details that well. But I believe there were some references that OG Vlasic's headquarters were in Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D133, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, answering a question of mine yesterday, namely, whether you knew that in some cases individual SJBs or entire police complements were placed under the military command, you said that you didn't know or weren't sure that anything like that happened. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that from the military documents that entire SJBs were placed under the command of the military. At least not from the Krajina documents. I did obviously accept there was a comment in a document that you showed me yesterday that that was ... a complaint.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the entire police complement in a certain area was placed under the control of the military?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which area in particular are you talking about, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In certain brigade zones or specifically in the zone of responsibility of the brigade commanded by Mr. Peulic. That is the 122nd Light Infantry Brigade, or the 343rd Motorised Brigade, which conducted activities in the general area of Dubica and Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't agree with that. I don't see documents that Colonel Peulic made that clear in the references that I have seen in the Krajina documents. He doesn't seem to make that clear in the references in the Crisis Staff, Kotor Varos Crisis Staff, documents. He didn't seem to make that clear as being the case when he referenced the incident on Vlasic mountain which occurred in his zone, and General Talic didn't make that except for that one reference I've talked about with Mr. Krgovic [sic] on the 1st of July, which I don't see as being implemented. So I wouldn't agree with you that the military commanders believe that in the entire zone -- their zone that the police are under their command. Far from it. I see numerous references about cooperating with them rather than them being subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let us take another look at 1D406. That's tab 28 in the Zupljanin Defence binder. I believe it was tendered by Mr. Zecevic but I also have it in my binder. That's the order dated the 1st of July. This is the order where Mr. Talic orders --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the following page -- or, rather, the first reference is to the 343rd Motorised Brigade under item 1, and under item 4, the 122nd Light Infantry Brigade is referred to. Could we please go to the following page now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You see this paragraph toward the bottom. In the conduct of combat activities all police forces, and I repeat, all police forces, shall be placed under the command of the zone commander who shall decide how they are used." Mr. Brown, isn't this a clear-cut case of an order where General Talic orders that all police forces in the above-mentioned zones shall be placed under the command of the zone commander, and some ten days later, there's Mr. Zupljanin's presentation in which he objects to his practice, this practice?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I've discussed this document before, and there's an ambiguity in the document and in the reference. It may well be what is he discussing here is that after the agreements that were articulated in May and June that police formations can be subordinated or used in combat operations that he -- he is saying that under those circumstances where they are involved in combat operations, zone commander as -- has the right to -- placed under his command. I don't read this as being him or the one reading is I don't read it as being him saying that wherever policemen are in the zones of the various zone commanders articulated, that all police in combat operations are to be subordinated there, because after this document -- it's not reechoed in any other document I noticed in the Krajina Corps collection, and after this document, the same process of requesting support appears to have been in place. We've seen, for example, the documents in November or October where that's the case, and the references that I have seen about combat operations do not specifically reference specific police units, so for example the Kotor Varos Light Brigade document at the end of July does not have a reference to a specific police company or formation that the commander is ordering. The references continue to be, after this, of cooperation with the police and a process by which if -- if -- if police -- additional police support is required, it has to be agreed through the command and the police authorities. So I -- I flag this document up myself in the report. It does seem to be a slight anomaly. It does appear to have different readings to it. But I don't see after this that is there any change that zone commanders or commanders subordinate to General Talic are doing anything other than they were before which was cooperating with the police and in exceptional circumstances making formal requests or requesting police support, which in some cases was granted. So I don't read this as being, irrespective of what it says, either it was actually implemented in that manner that all zone commanders commanded police. I see it potentially meaning or potentially there was a problem he wanted to address or that it was a reemphasis to say that once there was agreement and police were placed at the -- for the use of the military that it was the zone commander who was the one that was to decide how they were to be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I reviewed your report thoroughly, including the footnotes. Until the month of September and possibly until October, I was unable to find a single document in which requests are made to the CSB to use units or any sort of application to the corps command as provided for by rules and regulations to address the CSB and request for -- requests -- resubordination of units. That practice only starts in September but before that I haven't seen a single document corroborating what you're saying that requests actually had been made. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, no. Can I make the same, please, objection as I made with Mr. Zecevic. That's a speech. It is irrelevant what Mr. Krgovic has found or hasn't found. It's not a question at all, it's a comment. And how is the witness supposed to answer that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is clearly a question. I haven't found it and I asked the witness whether he has any reference to show me the contrary. What I'm saying is that from the outbreak of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina up until the autumn of 1992, have you found a single document where a corps command requests something from the CSB? I'm referring to the spring and the summer, until that letter by Mr. Zupljanin dated 18 September.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look at my documents and I don't know them all. It may be that document -- there was -- that express need. I do know there was formed police units in the operation corridor. Now, what the process behind that was and what was requested, I'm not sure. And I would have to check my references again. But the -- the process as laid down in May and June was that requests should be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it may well have been that in the spring --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I must interrupt you. You will have an opportunity to review these documents. I haven't found any, but you can possibly continue about this after the break. But let us move onto another topic. In your report, you deal with the issue of the CSB special unit which you mention several times. You were -- you cited some documents, so please take a look at -- please bear with me. The reference is 281; footnote 414. You cite a document of the Crisis Staff here; that is, the minutes taken at the Crisis Staff meeting, and you say that that document is about the event that happened in front of the health centre. It's Exhibit P46; tab 29 of the Zupljanin Defence. Please take a look at this document which you cited. Also there footnote 359 it says in item 2: "Within the framework of this item, events were discussed which occurred in the course of the day, which was considered the most serious since the outbreak of the war in Kotor Varos. The final outcome of today's fighting is still unknown. In the health centre, six people have been registered as killed and 19 wounded." Obviously, this is about killed and wounded Serbs who were provided medical assistance in the health centre and not about Muslims or Croats, as you say.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure my report says it is Muslims or Croats. I think my report says one of the minutes which was the 40th made mention that the CSB had been engaged in unauthorised behaviour, and that this session mentioned that six people had been killed and wounded and around the health centre. And my report isn't to look at the details of the -- the actual incident although I'm aware of it, not -- not in depth, but my report was making the issue that they were aware that there had been unauthorised behaviour there and that people had been killed in the health centre. If your position is that those people are Serbs and the wounded were Serbs, then the document doesn't say one way or the other, but I do know there was an incident, a somewhat notorious incident at the health centre involving the CSB, allegedly. My report isn't about the incident, per se, in terms of the detail of it. It's just that the Crisis Staff were clearly aware of this incident and that it allegedly involved the CSB special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But the document you cite in footnote 414 and which you link to unauthorised behaviour is something altogether different from the incident in front of the health centre which happened some days earlier. I believe that's obvious from the document.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, is your issue that there are two separate incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know the chronology of the crime base incidents in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when, in this paragraph 2.80, and in footnote 415, you speak about things and you remember that you discussed this report with the Prosecutor too, so let me quote to you your words: "The massacre of the -- of members of a special police detachment in Kotor Varos municipality has additionally aggravated interethnic relations in the area and made the overall security situation more complex."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could I have the page number in the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's paragraph 280 in Mr. Brown's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, you commented for the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, no, I'm sorry that's why I got a bit confused. What's happening there it's not Mr. Brown's words he is quoting the VRS document. That's why I got a bit confused. If one looks at the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Korner, please let me finish. I have just read out this part and now I'd like to -- so in the previous footnote, answering to the Prosecutor's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On page 18760 you said that this section you quoted was a mistake. That this wasn't a massacre of the special police but the other way around. It's a massacre of Muslims and Croats conducted by the special police. Do you remember saying that? If you want, I can show you the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter 3707. It's tab 18 in the Zupljanin Defence binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm not trying to interrupt Mr. Krgovic, but it read, and the question was put as though Mr. Brown was making that assertion, that it aggravated interethnic relations. At the report at page 280 says: "This incident was later reported as a massacre in a 1st Krajina Corps daily combat report to the Main Staff." There is then a quote from that combat report which is what Mr. Krgovic read to him, which is then footnoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a reference in paragraph 2.50. That's where Mr. Brown claims that this report by the Krajina Corps refers to the incident that happened in front of the health centre and where the Muslims were victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your understanding of this document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding of this Krajina Corps document is that it's referring to the activities of the special police unit, not a massacre that's happened to them. I -- I don't know the full details of the CSB and what they were doing, but I was not aware that the CSB unit was massacred or had a significant -- significant combat casualties. That doesn't seem to be made note of in the minutes at the Kotor Varos Crisis Staff. So my assumption is that the CSB -- they may have had casualties, I don't know, but they were not portrayed as having had a massacre done on them. And my inference from the comments of the -- the two comments of the Kotor Varos Crisis Staff staff meetings and the reference in the Krajina Corps document a number of days later is that they are referencing a massacre at the Kotor Varos -- I'm sorry, the special unit of the CSB conducted and that that massacre is aggravated interethnic relations. That's how I read this. If you have documents that the CSB were massacred in Kotor Varos, I'm happy to comment on those, but I -- I read this as the massacre has been perpetrated by the special unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, paragraph number 3, in this order clearly states that the massacre was perpetrated on the members of the police. There is no doubt in this text.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, sir, that's what the document reads. My own view of this in light of the information I've just discussed is that -- that -- that this is either a typing error or a misreporting, and I -- from what I know, I do not believe this is a massacre that has been perpetrated on the CSB but it is referencing the problem that has been caused because of the incident involving the CSB. And it's a combat report, sir, not an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, would you take a look at 2D08-0119, which is tab 34 in the Zupljanin binder. It's a monograph listing members of the Ministry of Interior who were killed together with the dates of their deaths and their pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the front page. Can I have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at Milan Ivkovic. Centre of public security Banja Luka, killed on the 29th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then Nenad Kalamanda, centre of public security from Banja Luka, killed on 29th June, 1992 and then Zeljko Kukic. And he was a member of the police station in Kotor Varos.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Slavisa Marinkovic. Banja Luka public security centre, killed on 29th of June 1992. And then Zoran Racic. Public security centre Banja Luka, killed on 29th of 6th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Predrag Stokuca, public security centre Banja Luka, killed on 29th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Drazenko Savic, public security centre Banja Luka, killed on 29th June 1992. Then Dragisa Stanivukovic. Also public security centre Banja Luka killed on 29th June 1992. These were the killings discussed at this meeting in Kotor Varos when they talk about the people killed on 29th of June, they say that the fighting on that date was very fierce and that there were five or six killed and 1999 injured so far in the fighting and that's the people that they are talking about. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I'm sure -- it may well be that Mr. Krgovic is right but he is making the assertion. All that we can see at the moment is that these people were killed. What's the link between that and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: On a particular date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On a particular date. Well, can I just ask -- I mean, I'm sure Mr. Krgovic is right but what is the evidence of the link.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I can make the link. It's just starting point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you -- in answer to your question, if -- if these individuals were all killed in Kotor Varos on that day in combat operations, you may well be right. Obviously it lists their names and where they came from and what -- what unit they were from. Under the circumstances of how they were killed is not clear to me but you may well be right. This is the first time I have seen this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, sorry, but if this would have been people killed in -- policemen killed in combat operation, would military report speak of a massacre or of killings? Is this for -- for -- for military people a massacre, if it's killing in combat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- I have seen other references where the 1 Krajina Corps used the phrase "massacre" for the killing of Serbs. For example I think there was an ambush of policemen in Mrkonjic Grad earlier in the war, quite early on. I think a group of policemen travelling in an area with some military were ambushed and killed. That was called a massacre as opposed to killings in a combat zone and so that was one other example. I mean, at times they used that phrase "massacre" when they talk about killings of their own. They don't necessarily differentiate between -- sometimes or in that one case. They may well have used the phrase "massacre" when actually people were conducting combat operations as we would recognise that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have P45. That's a video about this event, and I want it placed from 12:02.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have an English transcript here so that you can follow the names and the events.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "it is very difficult to get to the bodies of the dead soldiers, much mor difficult than the fighting itself. This is when the blackmail starts. The enemy first mutilates the dead body, cuts the face, gouges out the eyes, cuts off the head and invariably asks for several live extremists in exchange for the body of a dead and mutilated Serb. So the bodies of the dead soldiers were only delivered today. The enemy used blackmail and demanded all sorts of things." Policeman speaking: "We got our comrades back after three days. We complied with all the requests they put to us. They asked us to bring a hodja's son who had not even been arrested. We went to the yard, to the town, brought him, made an offer. They asked for 17 of the living in exchange for our number of dead. We gave them to them. And look what they returned to us. Our men mutilated and burnt. And we shall pay them back. We shall remember and pay them back for this." Reporter: "Could you identify the dead and mutilated combatants?" Second Policeman: "By their uniforms." Question: "Only by their uniforms?" Answer: "Yes." Another Policeman: "The lads were mutilated, their eyes gouged out, their heads set on fire, and the rest." Reporter: "They did that, gouged out the eyes and burned the heads of Serb fighters. And so, after several days the bodies of the dead soldiers were here today." A Policeman: "My best friends."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, they speak here about the massacre of the members of the special unit of the police. You could also see their dead bodies. So, isn't that a very accurate interpretation what we find in the report by the Krajina Corps that a group of the members of the special police had been massacred by the members of Muslim and Croat forces in Kotor Varos, and that that's what caused interethnic tensions. Wouldn't you then agree that what it says in the combat report is accurate and what it says in your report is inaccurate, which also leads us to the conclusion that a number of your conclusions that you made based on this are also inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could you pause there, please, Mr. Krgovic. You have -- there's nothing wrong with the propositions that you put to the witness. It's just that they -- one builds on the other, and I think in fairness to the witness and to the Chamber to understand it, we should get his answers one at a time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, the last is no more than a speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But if you read the report carefully, you will see that if you interpret this document in this particular way, you will arrive at a number of conclusions. We are certainly going to go through all these conclusions and the witness is certainly going to have a chance to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One question for you, Mr. Brown. Isn't it true, based on what you've seen, the two documents that you have seen, isn't it true that your interpretation of the report of the 1st Krajina Corps is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm prepared to accept that that could be a modified assessment. Now, whether you would describe the action and the ambush as a massacre, or whether would you describe it as an unfortunate occurrence in a combat zone, is something, you know, maybe different. But I'm more than prepared to -- to modify my assessment that clearly there was an incident, how it was described and what reaction is a separate issue, and I'm more than happy to amend my -- my -- my reference that the Krajina Corps was making reference to the incident in which policemen, local and CSB policemen, were killed. That's one issue. Do I think that that -- I think one of your questions was in relation to ethnic tensions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This incident, an incident in which Serbs were killed caused interethnic tensions and not the other way around. So your conclusion is wrong. The tensions arose because of a crime committed on Serbs, not on Muslims.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I wouldn't necessarily agree with that. I wouldn't doubt that that incident in itself could and would cause tensions. But the operation that was going on at the time, I would argue was linked to the operational instructions of some weeks back that there was a desire to take control of Kotor Varos municipality through the documentation that, for example, came out on the 9th of June and that Kotor Varos was seen as an area that needed to be controlled and operations were mounted in Kotor Varos. Now, as part of that operation, I would accept that it seems that some policemen were killed there. That in itself might well have inflamed -- inflamed the situation further. I would imagine that type of video, if it's going out on TV, is also likely to further aggravate the circumstance. But I wouldn't agree with your -- your assumption that interethnic tensions in Kotor Varos started or were caused because of that incident. They certainly would have done nothing, I would assume, to reduce it, but that incident, I would argue has to be placed in the context of the desire to control Kotor Varos municipality that fell from instructions prior to this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, didn't you cite this document by the 1st Krajina Corps and used it as an example of an incident in which members of the special police massacred Muslim population which then led to the aggravation of interethnic tensions. Isn't that your interpretation of the document while the actual situation is the other way around and you made a mistake while evaluating this document and while deriving your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm more than prepared to amend that document -- inference based on the pictures that you've shown of those individuals in that war book. I'm more than happy to amend that. I do not -- as I said to you in the beginning, this report has limitations. I didn't see every single document, I hadn't seen that war book of the fallen before. So I'm more than happy to amend that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I didn't see or hear anything on this video that links the video to the report and the killings you referred to on the 29th of June. I'm sure there is, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I was simply trying to save time. I'm going to continue with the same video. I think it's 9:59.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There's a transcript. It's your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Second page, just -- go to next paragraph in English. After this. Next paragraph. It's tab 93. We can find the name of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's my fault. My -- the translation of the video, the transcript, my copy stops and I don't know if the one in e-court does with the bit that we just played, namely the gouging out of the eyes and all the rest of it. There's no further English. And Mr. Krgovic is going to play more of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a paragraph that follows the name. I have it in my copy. Mr. Brown has it in front of him. That's where you can find the names.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I see, we're going to replay it. Oh, I see, I'm sorry, yep.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Kozara, Grmec, Sator and other Bosnian Krajina mountains and hills are once again calling for revenge. utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Mr. Brown, you can see that we can find here all the names of the people that we found in the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You went too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, so we can find the seven names here, people killed on the 29th of June, 1992, whose bodies were then exchanged on the 4th of July, the same day that the report by the Krajina Corps was made. utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm more than happy to accept that's the case, sir, and I'm more than happy to amend my report in that respect. I don't think it alters my view in relation to the situation in Kotor Varos. The operations that were conducted as a result of documents prior to that, the reference to the Crisis Staff meetings and the incidents at the health centre which I believe was around 26th/27th. But I'm more than happy to amend that. There clearly was an incident later in which some policemen were killed or ambushed and killed, or whatever the circumstances were and that the Krajina Corps report of a few days later is referring to that ambush as opposed to other incidents. I'm more than happy to amend that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then further on, your conclusion, in paragraph 2.50, where you interpret this order dated 1st of July by General Talic, places under his command the police, and then delegates that authority to the military commanders, that is in the same paragraph and rests on the same conclusion.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'm more than happy to amend that conclusion, sir, as well, based on that information. I don't know whether the incidents and activities in Kotor Varos had a -- had a -- had a bearing on that more generally. Maybe the CSB police units were -- well, I'm more than happy to amend that position too, sir, or drawing that inference in relation to that incident in the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour, the only -- I'm just raising it now and I say it again, of course, it's a matter for Your Honours, but at the moment we've got on the 29th of June, these six or seven people being killed and we've got a video that they're members of the special police. I'm still not clear how it is said to be those that we discussed outside the health centre. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Do you have any evidence of this, Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this should be sufficient. All these documents that I have submitted should be convincing enough for Ms. Korner. The problem stems from that the fact there was an erroneous of an interpretation of a report mentioned in a report by the 1st Krajina Corps and then Ms. Korner made a wrong interpretation and derived wrong conclusions. There was no massacre in front of the health centre. That's why I'm trying to focus on this. Of course, the Court is going to deliberate on this. We are certainly going to bring more participants in these events to elaborate on the details, but I think that for the time being, my explanation should be sufficient. Or, rather, the evidence I have submitted so far. I don't have enough time to go into details. This is simply one of the segments of my examination. I have more videos and more documents but I don't have time at this particular moment. There are more important things that I still want to go through. Mr. Brown accepted that he would change something that Ms. Korner would not change, but that's really her own discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not trying to persuade Mr. Krgovic to carry on with this, but I'm simply pointing out that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. It's comment.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone not on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the document in footnote 34, 2D08-0119. I would like that admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D134, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a short digression, Mr. Brown, but we are actually still dealing with the subject of resubordination. In answer to a question by Mr. Zecevic you mentioned the police brigade operating in November 1992. In the reporting chain and the chain of responsibility according to the doctrine and the practice that was in force at the time, to whom did that brigade report? Or, rather, to whom its commander reported and sent his combat reports to?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know because I don't have the archive of that brigade, but I would assume they would -- they would -- they would pass it to the superior operational group commander in the zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You know that this brigade, although it was formed by the request of the 1st Krajina Corps and sent outside the zone of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, was actually in the complement of the East Bosnia Corps commanded by General Simic. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, sir, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you a document. 2D07-1144.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we are not getting a document on e-court. Ah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, this is a regular combat report of the command of the police brigade from the CSB Banja Luka. You see on the right-hand side who it is being sent to, the command of the Eastern Bosnia Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem that that's the case. Whether between its establishment it was moved to the command of the East Bosna Corps or what change may have happened, I don't know, or whether, at that particular time in December he was instructed to pass combat reports to the East Bosna Corps commander, I don't know. But it may well have been that it was moved or actually placed upped the command of the East Bosna Corps, bearing in mind that the East Bosna Corps had a significant part to play in -- in operations in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Further on, when you were responding to Mr. Zecevic's questions yesterday about the police brigade from the Republic of the Serb Krajina, the RSK, do you know that roughly it was the same. They were included in the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska but they were officially the police brigade of the RSK with the same kind of rights and responsibilities, like the police brigade from Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the details of the RSK MUP's engagement. All I know is that they were certainly present in operations in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see paragraph 2 of this order? This is what it says: "During the day, units of the brigade went to reconnoitre enemy positions and organised defence and heightened security of redeployment areas particularly in the area that was taken over from the 3rd Battalion of the police brigade of the RSK, the Republic of the Serb Krajina." So in fact they were a police brigade just like they were the Banja Luka brigade, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem that they had been given a designation like that. This is a report, by the way, not an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: A report. I don't know if I misspoke at some point, but I agree, it is a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, in your report and in your testimony, when answering Ms. Korner's questions, you spoke of a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown P611; Prosecution tab 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Remember this? It's the state of combat morale in the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: See this paragraph here? "All units and armed formations have essentially been put under the control of the 1st Krajina Corps although there is still resistance from the CSB ..." It's at the very top of the page in the English version. If I understood your interpretation correctly, you said that basically this observation has to do with the special unit of the CSB of Banja Luka and that it had not been placed under the control -- remember, it doesn't have to do with Prijedor. Judge Harhoff also asked you about your interpretation of this. So my question would be the following. Do you know this document of the 3rd of September? Namely, that the unit, the special unit, the detachment of the CSB Banja Luka had been disbanded a month before that and placed under the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, and that your understanding of this document is erroneous?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, could you -- are you saying that the CSB had been disbanded?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The unit, the special police detachment that you spoke of, had been disbanded a month before this report and placed under the corps command.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that -- and again, I don't know the details in terms of the MUP but I know that there had been a move to disband the CSBs and that that had been internally resisted, at least initially, because I believe there was some demonstrated need. So at the regional level I believe there was some resistance to having the CSB disbanded but I do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know the details of it -- I do know -- well, I don't know if they were subsequently disbanded and integrated into the military or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, are you referring to the special units of the CSB or the CSB as such?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: CSB special units, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, rather, could the witness be shown P1252, tab 21 of the Zupljanin Defence. 1502, sorry. P1502.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I don't know if have you this document. I don't think you do. This is a report on a visit to the Security Services Centre by MUP officials from headquarters. And look at number 1, the conclusion. Actually, it's on page 2 in English. Paragraph 1, where it says that: "The special police detachment, 100 men strong, will be put at the disposal of the 1st Krajina Corps under the command of General Talic as of the 10th of August 1992." And then, further on, paragraph 2: "The handover of the unit will be carried out on the 10th of August at 8.00 in Kotor Varos where the unit is deployed. The handover will be attended by Djuro Bulic SJB sector chief, on behalf of the CSB, and by Colonel Bogojevic, military security chief, on behalf of the 1st Krajina Corps. " And then the second paragraph of item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I shall paraphrase, but in the territory of the centre, that is to say, in the area of the public security station there are no special police units or any other units. That is to say that from that moment onwards there is no special unit. It has been placed under Talic's command. You will agree with me that your interpretation of this document is erroneous on the basis of the previous document that I had shown you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time I have seen this document and I wouldn't necessarily say that it indicates a contradiction between the assessment report that you showed me first. And I would have to read both of them together. But the assessment report written, I believe, in September, is an assessment of the state of morale for August so it is looking back at the situation in August. Now -- and it's saying -- I'm assuming it is referencing or referring to that this unit should have been integrated into the military but that problems, despite this instruction presumably, despite this instruction, that problems are still existing in that regard. So although the morale report is dated September, it is referring, I assume -- and, again, I would have to read them both together -- I haven't read this document before, but it may well be that this was what was to be agreed, but in reality there still remained problems that hadn't been resolved when the morale of the -- the officer who wrote the Krajina Corps report stated that all units and formations had been brought in but there are still problems with this. So it doesn't necessarily disagree with me -- my -- my -- my point that the corps still felt there were problems in this regard. But I'd have to -- I'd like to read this document in its entirety and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You will have an opportunity do so. I'm going to print the document out in English and you will have the opportunity of seeing both documents during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if this would be the right time for the break, I would kindly ask that we take the break now, which would mean that it's a few minutes early, but I would like to be able to give the expert these documents so that he could prepare for the rest of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask whether Mr. Krgovic is able to give an indication of how much longer he's going to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was about to ask the same question. Indeed I was going to suggest that during the break if counsel can -- if Mr. Krgovic and Ms. Korner could meet and report when we come back, because even with the extended session, I'm wondering - and perhaps my apprehension is wholly unwarranted - but having regard to what Mr. Krgovic has indicated in terms of the numbers of matters into which he still intends to go, whether it is realistic to think of completing this witness, as I said, even with the extended session. But counsel would speak and report when we get back. So -- because the report would so indicate, if that unfortunate event were to occur, where we go from there. So we return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we've discussed -- sorry. We discussed how long Mr. Krgovic is going to be. He thinks the full next session, plus possibly a little bit of the last session. I estimate - and I know that my estimates are notoriously bad - but I estimate about an hour's worth of re-examination. So depending on Your Honours' number of questions, if any you have for the witness, we should be able to finish with an extra session today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, the witness who would have been walking in and heard the last part of your comment I'm sure is relieved to hear that. Yes, Mr. Krgovic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, I hope that you had an opportunity to see all of this document during the break, the document that I had showed you.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you manage to see it? On the basis of this document, on the 10th of August, the special unit of the CSB Banja Luka was transferred to the corps and placed under its command; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the -- from the document, that would seem to be what was -- what was requested or -- or to be decided. I mean, quickly trying to look at the document in some kind of context and I haven't seen the other references or some of the other references noted in the document it would seem that this is one of the documents that -- or sequence of events that may have fallen from that general issue of paramilitaries on the 28th of July and trying to bring groups under the command of the army that fall into that category. Because, on the 28th of July, there is a reference in that document that some members of the SOS, for example, are in the -- the CSB Banja Luka special unit and then possibly the sequence of events from this, just based on the document you've shown me there, is that there is this desire to bring that unit under the command of the army. There clearly is a meeting or some decision around that time as well, 27th of July, from the minister of the interior. There's obviously a series of meetings that go on in Banja Luka in early August in relation to, presumably, what to do with the special unit, Banja Luka Special Unit, and I think there's presumably some kind of hesitancy that this should be integrated into the army, at least from the reference, because it says that platoon commanders and members of special units rejected the suggestion. Then clearly there's a decision after that meeting that this unit should be placed under the command of the army and this is to be done in Kotor Varos on -- on the 10th of -- 10th of August. But as I said earlier, it may well be the reference in the morale report for August is referring to the fact that, despite this, there was still some difficulties or problems, maybe reflecting what's said at paragraph 3 of the document that some individuals, members of the special unit themselves, rejected the initial idea of being placed under the army. So maybe that is my reading of the context of this document, but I don't know all the background to the workings of the Banja Luka Special Police Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, Mr. Brown, that towards the end of July 1992, at the level of all of Republika Srpska, all of these special units were disbanded on the basis of an order issued by the minister in order to establish a single special unit in the MUP and that that was actually the reason why these units were disbanded?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please switch off microphones that are not being used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I'm not an expert on the issue of the MUP and their special units and the reasons behind their disbandment or formation. As I said, maybe my brief reading of this document, bearing in mind the timing in the military documents and some of the references contained in it, is that there was a desire, bearing in mind what seemed to be at least from the military document that there are some undesirables within the CSB special -- Banja Luka special unit that it should be placed under the command of the army. And maybe the document in September talking about what was happening in August was that that wasn't completely successful or at least there were still some issues to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, when you dealt with the participation of police units in combat operations, you said, in paragraph 248 of your report, you talked about cooperation or joint operations between the police and military in the municipalities of Banja Luka, Sipovo and Jajce. Do you know on the basis of which principle these operations were carried out? Were police units resubordinated to a specific military unit with a view to carrying out certain operations? When you say "joint operations" or "cooperation," is that what you meant in terms of cooperation between the military and the police, based on the principle of resubordination?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I've discussed that at length earlier on. I would have to go into the individual references about Sipovo and Banja Luka and Jajce but I'm assuming what I've done is referenced the phrases that the army used, which is "cooperation," "joint operations." I think I have covered that quite exhaustively in the last two or three days. Most of the references I see in the military documents, or many of them refer to "in cooperation," "in concert ."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically when you speak about Jajce, you're talking about coordinated action. You're not talking about resubordination. Do you know which form this took, these operations around Jajce? What kind of police participation was there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, sir. I don't know the details of the very large operation that occurred later in 1992 in -- in Jajce. I didn't go into every -- every area. I would have to look at the references that I have got in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going show you a document, P411, paragraph 13 in Prosecution tab 69. Sorry. Defence tab, Stanisic Defence tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 262.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is one of the first documents that I found, if I can put it that way, from October, which treats things lawfully. That is to say, how resubordination should be carried out. You see here a document of Mr. Zupljanin's. You see the preamble where it says: "Pursuant to a request from the command of the 1st Krajina Corps of the Army of Republika Srpska to engage 158 members of the police from the Banja Luka CSB region, who will be resubordinated to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, to execute designated tasks in Jajce." It is obvious that this operation in Jajce involved police participation on the basis of resubordination; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And have I never said that police could not be subordinated to the military. This would seem to be another example where there clearly was some agreement, some request from the Krajina Corps which was accepted by the CSB, and that police individuals from these municipalities were to be engaged in combat operations presumably in -- in trying to liberate, as they often referred to it, liberate Jajce, which was successfully done. Clearly there's been agreement and it's been accepted and the police are to be -- Mr. Zupljanin is instructing or ordering, ordering his subordinate police units, to -- to go and place themselves within the Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As for the system of commanding subordinated units you know that in accordance with the then doctrine of the JNA and the Army of Republika Srpska there was the principle of singleness of command and subordination. So there's a single commander and there's a single chain of command. There are no parallel chains of command.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's a general principle of unity of command, yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This unit, when it is resubordinated to the 1st Krajina Corps, receives orders directly from the military commander in that chain of command; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect so. I don't know what the agreements were, but the -- that -- I would imagine the police units were given to -- given a particular area or to a particular commander as agreed by the police and by the -- by the -- by the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you about this anymore. My colleague Mr. Zecevic devoted quite a bit of time to this principle of resubordination, so I'm going to move onto something else. There was something I wanted to discuss with you in relation to your analysis, the one that we have here. Mr. Brown, in your analysis, you spoke in detail about the 5th Corps, that is to say, whether the JNA still existed in the territory of the Bosnian Krajina and then the relationship with the SDS and the local certain authorities, the Serb side, if I can put it that way, with the JNA. You talked about that relationship, as it were. What about the members of the SDA and the Muslim people? What was their attitude towards the JNA in the area and towards the mobilisation that was carried out in 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I deal with the issue of the mobilisation in 1991 first, I do know that a large number of Muslims and Croats did not respond to the mobilisation. Some did, and obviously those JNA members that were already serving, continued to serve. Generally, there are comments that in 1991, for the operations in Croatia, you know, there were people who did not respond to the mobilisation. And it's not an area that I looked at in great depth in terms of numbers or statistics, but there were issues more widely with the response of non-Serbs to -- to the mobilisation. But some did respond, I have to say. Sorry, your second area was in relation to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: SDA.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I -- the report was not an analysis of the -- you know, the -- the political workings of the SDA or -- or their forces. But I -- I'm more to happy to concede there were problems of mobilisation, non-Serbs in '91, for operations in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of this official call of the SDA? As a matter of fact, President Izetbegovic that Muslims and Croats should not respond to mobilisation in JNA units? This is 1992.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure of the details, but it would not surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it's precisely for that reason that, inter alia, the structure was changed, the structure of the members of the JNA in the area, which contributed to a significant decrease in the number of Croats and Muslims in the JNA, in relation to the number of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, clearly, if reservists are not responding to the mobilisation that would alter the actual structure of units, yes. It may not have been so prevalent certainly in the early months of 1992 or even actually for the war in Croatia in 1991. It may not have been so prevalent for active members of the JNA from non-Muslim ethnicities. I do know there was a problem, as I say, of mobilisation and undoubtedly that might have meant that units were short and that, you know, the -- the balance would have been affected. That's not to say that non-Muslims in entirety didn't respond, because I believe some of them did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I meant non-Serbs, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: With regard to the period preceding this, the share of Muslims and Croats in the JNA was negligible, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say whether it was negligible or not. I mean, there were other problems. It wasn't just that mobilisation of non -- Muslims and Croats was a problem. I think there were also problems that, bearing in mind the JNA was a federal body of individuals from ethnicities in Serbia, Serbs from Serbia who also didn't respond to the mobilisation. So it wasn't a case that all Serbs responded in the whole of the FRY and that non-Serbs didn't. But I -- as I say, I'm happy to -- to -- to concede there was clearly a problem of the mobilisation. I mean, I think a lot of Croats in particular were unhappy with what was going on in Croatia and the operations in Croatia, so it was probably reasonable for many of them to feel that they didn't want to fight in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Speaking about the military situation in general, in the area of Krajina which borders on Croatia, but also beyond, the 5th Corps transferred some of its units from Western Slavonia to Bosnia-Herzegovina and the reason being - and I believe you mentioned that in your report - to prevent the war from spilling over from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was one of the reasons for transferring the units from Western Slavonia to Bosnia-Herzegovina, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- it's probably one of the reasons. I mean, there was agreement, UN agreement, a UN-brokered agreement, I forget the exact dates, but I think it was the early part of 1992 that the JNA should withdraw anyway. So they were obligated to withdraw. But General Talic phases that withdrawal and some units were withdrawn early and I believe in some of his documents he was -- you know, moves them back into areas, and I think even in some of his documents references to prevent interethnic conflict. I don't shy away from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what essentially happened was that the war did spill over from Croatia to Bosnia-Herzegovina because the first conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a consequence of Croatian forces crossing the border carrying out some activities and killing some people, such as Sijekovac in March 1992 and Malovan near Kupres and those were the first clashes, military clashes in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sijekovac is near Bosanski Brod, by the way.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the fine detail of chronology and I will defer to you. I know there were clashes in Bosanski Brod and the -- there were Croatian, mainly Croatian populated municipalities in the area and there were clashes and problems. But there were also clashes and problems in other areas, so in -- if you talk about March that -- that may well have been the case there, but there were clashes in Bijeljina, for example, and in -- in late March and early April. So it wasn't necessarily simply that -- the area that you mentioned in Bosanski Brod. I believe there were other areas around that time too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, talking about the military situation in the Bosnian Krajina, answering a question of the Prosecutor, you said that you didn't analyse the operations of the Muslim and Croatian forces in that area because that wasn't your task, but, rather, that you focussed on the operations of the 1st Krajina Corps in the territory controlled by it. I hope I correctly understood that answer that you gave Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I didn't avoid the issue completely. As I say, the collection was a JNA/VRS collection and they clearly made references to, in some cases, specific incidents, so for example the ambush of soldiers coming back in Kljuc. There were smaller incidents. They also reference sometimes generically that non-Serbs are armed and there are armed groups operating in certain areas. But I didn't specifically go into looking at the ABiH, for example or... That wasn't within really the brief of the report. But, undoubtedly, there were non-Serbs who were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, talking about the military situation in an area, if my understanding is that your report is to present the military situation in an area, isn't it necessary to present data about the enemy forces too? Because that would be required to paint a complete picture of the military situation and explain why this or that had to be done. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would agree. I mean, clearly, if I had, you know, if the -- if the brief that I was given was to include that, and also if the material was there, and I had an archive of the ABiH and wanted to do that, then -- then clearly it would be more complete. That really wasn't the function of the report. It was to look at the archive that had been collected. You know, I -- I have mentioned the limitations of the report and, you know, this is not an exhaustive study of everything relating to that. My analysis in relation to the issue of the arming of the non-Serb population or armed groups formed military formations from the ABiH or elsewhere, really is drawn from the Krajina Corps collection. There weren't many references. There wasn't a big intelligence file or brief outlining their view of what the non-Serbs were armed with, the breakdown of their companies or formations or groupings, even if you like, on the points of contact in places like Central Bosnia or in the corridor. They -- they make reference and often quite generically. But you know, I was working with the materials I had and my analysis in that area is based on that and the general conclusions I got was, yes, there was a severance of the corridor. Yes, there were clearly some Croatian units armed in the municipalities you talked about in -- in the corridor area, quite well armed. But, in relation to the municipalities that they took control of in the early period, those municipalities seemed to be reasonably uncoordinated. Control was taken really quickly. The references that they have to armed groups are often very sort of general and quite low-ish level. But that isn't to say that -- the non-Serb population were not conducting actions. They were. Maybe that's a long-winded way of answering your question, but I didn't look at it in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you dealt with the mobilisation in detail, or with the TO units, as far as I understood, in that phase before the creation of the VRS, the TO units were a regular military formations in the area and they had the status of combatants, just as the JNA, right? Whether it's the TO controlled by the Serb side or the Muslim side or the Croatian side. We're basically talking about armed forces there?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The TO was slightly more complicated, I think, in the 5th Corps, in that there was mobilised Territorial Defence units that had been mobilised for operations in Croatia and who were already working under the JNA. One of those, for example, would be the 6th Brigade from Sanski Most. So there was that component. And also in April there was, after the mobilisation instruction from the SRBiH, there was the Serbian TO, which seemed to mobilise additional personnel, presumably often linked to the SDS or the municipal authorities, and they gradually - or quite quickly, I think - developed in municipalities. So that when, for example, the 6th Brigade went back to Sanski Most, there was an existing Serbian TO unit there, and I think both of them were involved in operations in Sanski Most. But I guess the word "combatants" has a legal phrase but my understanding is that, yes, they were armed formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And TO members, whether we're speaking the Serb TO, or the Croatian TO, or the Muslim TO, had the status of combatants and the right to protection under the Geneva Conventions in case of being captured by the enemy side and becoming prisoners of war, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'd have to look at my Geneva Conventions again and -- but no -- if it's an armed formation they have protections, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, Mr. Brown, you also touch upon the armed resistance of non-Serbs in paragraph 2.196 and the following. And there's a reference to a mobilisation list and the footnote is 650. Let me show you the respective document. It's tab 45; 1D04-9510. The tab is -- the tab number is in Mr. Zecevic's binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You comment to this in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see the second page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 2.606 of your work, you say that there about 2400 names on that list. Although some individuals have not signed to certify that they received a mobilization call, and you also mention the weapons in possession of the persons on those lists. Can you see that in your report? I'm talking about the list of the Kozarac TO, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would seem to be what the document says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, based on your analysis of some additional documents, you concluded that the date of this document is some day in early May 1992; correct? This can also be found in paragraph 2.206 toward the end, the last sentence. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's what I wrote that it may well be around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean, it's a list. It is very incomplete and it doesn't necessarily articulate more than what it says on the document. It's ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, what do you seek to show with this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I seek to show the list of mobilised members of the Kozarac TO. The list shows the persons mobilised in May 1992 and the list contains 2400 names. I agree with Mr. Brown's remark that not all individuals have signed that they were mobilised to the Kozarac TO, but the list shows that at the moment when the conflict broke out in Kozarac, at least about 2.000 people were mobilised to the TO of Kozarac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but this is an matter that arises as a result of this, and I think and I'm sorry to raise it now I think for safety's sake Mr. Brown ought to just briefly leave court. Because we can't ask him to take his earphones off.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Sejmenovic gave evidence before this Court not very long ago. He was limited, of course, from our point of view to the matter of the adjudicated facts. However, as Mr. Krgovic knows, he gave lengthy, lengthy testimony about these lists in previous cases. He was not asked a single question by Mr. Krgovic about those lists, and think Your Honours might have had an explanation which would have been more assistance now that I heard -- I waited until I heard why Mr. Krgovic wants to put this in and he wants to put it in as evidence that 24,000 -- I'm sorry, 2400 were mobilised effectively by the Muslim. There is ample evidence that could have been given by Mr. Sejmenovic about this and had we known this was going to go in in this fashion then he would have been asked those questions. So if it is to go in for the purpose which Mr. Krgovic wants to put it in, then I'm going to invite Your Honours to allow us to recall Mr. Sejmenovic who has personal knowledge of these lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may reply. Could Ms. Korner give me a reference of -- to Mr. Sejmenovic's testimony showing that he wasn't asked? He was asked and he gave evidence that he didn't know about the strength or the members of the TO. Whereas Mr. Brown cites this document in his work, that's why I showed -- showed it to him. Mr. Aleksic examined Witness Sejmenovic. He did ask him a question about the strength of these units and the answer was that he had no knowledge about it. As Ms. Korner says, this is nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I didn't bring it in, because I didn't realise that it was going to come up. I do have the passage and can I assure Your Honours that if you look at the transcripts for either Stakic or the Brdjanin cases, he gave lengthy explanations about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't care about. He was -- [Interpretation] This witness testified viva voce and he said that he has no knowledge about it. Or, rather, he avoided answering. And he was called to testify about adjudicated facts, which did not refer to this, and yet we asked him about it. And Mr. Brown talks about this document in two paragraphs. He interprets it, he analyses the armaments and, of course, he is the person to ask about these things and through whom I wish to tender this document, and these are the grounds for my application to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the time being, notwithstanding what Ms. Korner has indicated in terms of what she proposes to do if this document is tendered, it seems to me that the basis for the admission at present is that the -- this is a document cited by the witness who is presently on the stand and it is one that Mr. Krgovic is questioning the basis on which he utilizes it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, no, no. I fully accept -- and if that was simply related to his report, but Judge Harhoff asked why it was being tendered and effectively it is being tendered to show that 2400 men were mobilised into what was effectively a Muslim territorial organisation. Your Honour, I will find the passage at the break that I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we have the witness back on the stand.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 1D04-5901 shall be given number 2D136.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, do you know that parallel to the mobilisation that was conducted by the Serb authorities in the territory of Krajina, to call them that, the Muslim side also performed a mobilisation in the territory of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I forget the date. Was it 5th, or 6th, or 7th or 8th of April. Round about that. But, in early April, I believe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you certainly know that, in line with that call-up, there was a request by the Muslim TO that the armaments that were -- that were formerly in the TO warehouses but was, at that moment, in the possession of the JNA to be handed over to the units of the TO of Bosnia-Herzegovina once the JNA starts pulling out?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the details of the mobilisation instruction. There were TO warehouses and in order to get weapons I'm assuming to go mobilise, they were requesting that fact. If that's the case. But I don't know the details of the -- of the -- the ABiH or the Bosnian government's mobilisation. I believe it was related to activities in Bijeljina and other areas, some period -- some days, actually, prior to that. There had been attacks in Bijeljina and I think around the period of the mobilisation also in Zvornik. But in relation to the -- what the mechanics of that mobilisation, I'm a little bit unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the MUP, the MUP of the SRBiH, that the Muslim Croat MUP, issued an order to attack JNA units during their attempts to pull out of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as to erect barriers or hinder them in that process, as a consequence of which a conflict flared up in the territory of the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that in the Krajina area there was during this period of uncertainty as to exactly what the JNA's position was going to be that there was unease that certain JNA units were to be pulled out of the Krajina and that that necessitated, I believe, a blockade of Banja Luka -- I will it was maybe one of the strategic units a rocket unit or something of that nature but that in the Krajina area there were -- there were certain -- certainly barricades established because they felt the JNA shouldn't leave. I'm not sure in your question whether you mean the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Are you talking about the government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
