utterances.text: Yes, exactly. I mean the Sarajevo authorities. I will show you the relevant document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D151; tab 95 in the Stanisic Defence binder. I referred to three tab numbers and that's why I needed some time to find the document; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, please take a look. The commander of the TO staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Colonel Hasan Efendic, from Sarajevo on 29th of April, orders that columns and units of the former JNA must be hindered in their attempts to leave the territory of BiH. And it says that military facilities in the wider area from which attempts are being made to remove equipment and materiel must be blocked. And then item 4 says: "Quickly plan and begin combat activities in the entire territory of the Republic of BH and coordinate them with the staffs of the TOs of the regions, counties, and the -- the republic." To me, this looks like a -- a call to wage war on the JNA and actually a sign for the start of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This order is based on a decision of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina of 27 April.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at face value, it would seem that the Bosnian government are unhappy with the fact that equipment and materiel that could be of use presumably to them is -- is being -- is being removed by the JNA and that they want -- and they believe that this is in contrary to agreement annotated at the beginning, and they believe that JNA columns or facilities should be blocked in order that that property is not -- is not taken away. Clearly in the last paragraph, they are -- they are anticipating combat operations. And bearing in mind the timing of this, this is the end of April. There already had been significant clashes and -- and conflicts in places like Zvornik and Bijeljina, Sarajevo, and -- and probably elsewhere, that they are -- they are preparing for that. I don't see it specifically as a direct war on the JNA. I -- I see it more along the lines of there's been an agreement. They don't believe that agreement has been honoured, whatever that was, and the JNA are pulling out equipment that they think is either rightfully theirs or should be theirs and they are to block these convoys and facilities in order to stop that -- that happening. I know that subsequent to this, in May there were some convoys that were attacked, JNA convoys attacked. There was a very famous one, or infamous one, I suspect, in Sarajevo, in May, I believe, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, item 4 says: "Quickly plan and begin ..." So all the members of the TO are hereby ordered to begin combat activities in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's what it says. And clearly the -- the activities that have been going on in the previous weeks and the deterioration of the situation in Bosnia more widely has necessitated them to -- to -- to instruct that planning an operation to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, before this date, 30th of April, I have only analysed the municipalities mentioned in my client's indictment, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Teslic, Kotor Varos, Banja Luka, and in those territory, there were no armed clashes before this date. There were no attacks, and I also haven't found them in your report. There were just individual incidents. Everything that happened, happened after this date; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In general, most of the attacks in the Krajina, in terms of the municipality attacks, occurred from the middle or late May. Although there were takeovers of municipality, for example Prijedor. I know there was a takeover -- the SDS took over Prijedor actually properly on this date or if not the day after. This document also maybe needs to be placed in context what is happening with the declaration of an imminent threat of war and the mobilisation of the Serbs or the -- at least through the SDS which occurred, you know, a few days prior to this. So there is a contextual background. But, no, the attacks that you mentioned in those municipalities did occur generally in the middle - late May, June, and July, I suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So, except Kotor Varos, where the conflict broke up some time in June, in other municipalities Sanski Most, Prijedor and Kljuc, the conflicts broke up between approximately the 15th and the 30th of May, 1992. And it all had the same characteristics: Attacks on columns of the military passing through certain areas. That was a unifying characteristic of those attacks. They would attack columns at certain points, set up by the Muslim forces, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that is a pattern. I didn't see an attack on a column in Sanski Most. There was an incident that I know at a check-point in Hambarine in Prijedor in which two people were killed or a small number of people were killed. There was an attack in Kljuc at the end of May, I believe, in which a passing JNA bus was shot. And I think there was also a separate incident or maybe it was related I think when a policeman was killed. There was one incident, I remember, in Novi, I believe, I think a policeman or a military policeman and a policeman were killed, but that -- that was it, that I remember in detail. Sanski Most didn't have that, and Prnjavor didn't have that. Banja Luka, I don't remember having that. So I wouldn't agree with you that it was somehow a -- a pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When I say all these actions, although specifically in Prijedor it took part during the period of five or six days, in Kljuc as well. So bearing in mind the dates and the kind of the attack, to me, it tells that those attacks were synchronized.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't matter what it tells Mr. Krgovic. It's a question of the inferences that Your Honours draw and the witness should be asked a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking him whether that is true, whether my conclusion is correct. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't agree that that's the case especially when you place some of the contextual background of instructions through the chain to make plans for the disarmament of areas. Operations and planning operations were already going on, and certainly in some of those municipalities these minor and unfortunate incidents where people were killed did occur but I don't believe it appeared to me to be some coordination. Clearly there were ethnic tensions in these municipalities and incidents occurred, unfortunate incidents occurred, but I do believe that planning was already under way to take control of these territories, as articulated in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if you analyse a certain military situation in a certain region - let me now revert to my original intended question - in order to gain a clear insight into the strength of, for instance, a corps, and into the strength of the enemy, it would be necessary to take a look at the corps analysis for 1992. Isn't that so? So just as you commented on the combat-readiness analysis made at the level of the Main Staff with Ms. Korner, similar analysis were made at other levels, for instance, corps levels, so I would like that ask whether you had a chance to look at the analyse of the combat readiness of the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to go through my report again. I can't remember if there was one. I do remember there was one done from the 2nd Krajina Corps but I'm not sure I have got the one from the 1st Krajina Corps. It may be there, I have to see. I would have to check again. I think they all had to write one prior to the -- April 1993 one written by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: A question of general nature: In order to gain a complete picture of the events in the field and the military situation, it would be necessary to compare the forces, to make a comparison between enemy forces and a certain side forces, in order to gain a full insight into the situation.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think I have answered that previously. You know, in -- in -- if -- if the analysis was to contain absolutely everything, clearly, you know, documentary evidence, an analysis of the enemy, if that's the phrase, the enemy side would be valuable. That wasn't the nature of this analysis. It was focussed on the documents of the Krajina Corps and, you know, I make no apologies that that -- in some areas could be seen as a limitation. I go back to my, I think, the general thrust of the area about the non-Serb resistance or defence in that in those municipalities that you talked about and in the Krajina municipalities generally, control was established very quickly. That's not to say that the area of the corridor wasn't a problem, that that took a long time, a relatively long time, or months, I guess, in the end to completely expand it to the river although they were quite successful initially to get a route through, that is not to say in Jajce predominantly Croat defences were stubborn and resisted for a period of time. In part that is probably because of the terrain there, which is incredibly difficult from a military perspective; it's very mountainous. Maybe it's a testimony to the success of the corps that they even managed to take that territory. But I do look at it, generically, in that in particular with the municipalities and with the assets that the corps had and cooperation with the other organisations and civilian agencies and police that control seemed to be taken over in a matter of days, which leads me to the conclusion that the defences of these places at the time were not strong, were not coordinated, did not have significant weaponry, certainly in comparison to what is available to the -- to the army and the VRS, and I can only conclude that the defences were rudimentary at best, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, if we look at the strength of an enemy, a necessary element of such a analysis should be the casualties of the unit facing the enemy, isn't it? You are now describing the 1st Krajina Corps as a well-trained, well-armed and well-structured and organised unit; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would -- I would argue that it was -- I can't say for all the components and when they were mobilising individuals that -- the degree of training but it was a corps that had been in combat operations for a significant period of time and it did seem from the documents that they had a functioning command process and reporting process. And from the documents that I have seen, they were very well armed. They had armoured assets; they had tanks; they had artillery; they had aircraft; they had an air force in Banja Luka, and they had helicopters; they had a communication chain. So from that perspective it would seem to be a -- a well-functioning military corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If we talk about whether we could compare the strength of the sides in the conflict, you, as an analyst, what would you say, what would be a standard percentage of casualties of a certain unit, if the sides in the conflict are approximately equal? What is then the percentage of casualties on -- on one side, that we could say that it is an acceptable percentage of casualties or a normal per cent of casualties. I'm asking you that in case that you maybe performed some analysis besides this report that we are dealing with now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, where are we going with this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to show what are the parameters that could enable us to establish the strength of the enemy. He didn't analyse the strength of the Muslim side in his report or at least not enough to give us a real picture of their strength. I'm going to come to a specific example of the 1st Krajina Corps later. This was just an introductory question to find out what are generally accepted standards for that and then I'm going to go to a specific example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think to be honest, Mr. Krgovic, if this witness is unable to assess or to make any evaluation of the strength of the Muslim army at that time, I don't think it would help as much to try and draw an inference from the number of normal casualties from a general theoretical point of view. I don't think this will bring us any further to the truth. And, still, I have difficulties in fully understanding or appreciating the relevance of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my point is this: The witness did touch upon, to a certain extent, to the forces of the Muslims and Croats, and he basically describes them as unorganised and unarmed. So, now, what I wanted to find out with him, is if he talks specifically about casualties of the 1st Krajina Corps and I'm going to show documents later I would like to make a comparison, because the Defence certainly doesn't agree with this evaluation by the expert that Muslims and Croats were badly organised and unarmed and I'm now going to try to show this through the -- a report by the 1st Krajina Corps. The intention of my introductory question was to find out what are general standards. I don't know whether the witness can answer that question but the question is very simple. It is a introductory question which will then be followed by a specific question about a specific document and a specific analysis. And that's my last topic for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I think you should ask the witness then if he can inform us of the number of victims on each side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly yes, yes. I first wanted this specific thing. That was my intention but then I thought I would first go generally, find out the percentages in general and then later on go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, you heard this. Do you happen to know what are general standards about Courts percentage-wise when two forces of approximately the same strength are facing each other?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, I'm sorry, we're not going to go down that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: If you want to put a question to the witness relating to the number of casualties at a specific moment between the two sides of the conflict, then get on with that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, do you know what were the casualties of the Krajina Corps in 1992? And do you consider this -- excuse me. Do you consider that such an element would be important to analyse the military situation in Krajina in the relevant period?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the figures of casualties for the Krajina Corps of 1992. It may be something I could find out through going through all the documents. They undoubtedly took casualties. They -- in -- at times took, you know, not unsubstantial casualties. My assessment is that most of those casualties -- large numbers of casualties may have taken were as a result of operations in the corridor and Jajce, in particular. When you talk about casualties, if you say, Do I know what the casualties of the 1st Krajina Corps were for 1992, it would be very difficult for me to draw an inference about which operations, specifically, and where. They did suffer casualties. They do at times make reference to small -- smallish, in terms of numbers and we're talking, you know, five, six, seven, eight, in operations in the municipalities. So, for example, I believe, in Prijedor, General Talic made a reference to -- it may have been around eight or nine, maybe a few more or less, when he talked about congratulating the 343rd Brigade. I don't make the assertion that the armed -- well, I don't make the assertion that there were no armed formations on the non-Serb side. I don't make -- I can't comment on their organisation and structure because I haven't seen through the Krajina Corps documents many references to that. A lot of the time they refer to groups of individuals, small bands of individuals operating and we're talking about the municipality attacks. The -- from the documents I see in that period of May and into -- into June and specifically in the municipality areas, I do not see the corps took large numbers of casualties. I don't doubt they took large -- large -- but significant casualties up on the corridor area where I do believe that there was more of an organised and well-prepared defence in part because those municipalities had been -- or control of those municipalities had been taken over by, I believe, predominantly Croat forces and there were references to Croatian units coming over the border in to defend that. So it doesn't surprise me that the casualties were in the corridor area were noticeable and there were also, I have to say, references in the documents to self-inflicted casualties, and it seems to be a particular problem that they suffer where people go home, shoot friends or negligently discharge a weapon or a hand-grenade goes off and people are killed. There are references to that as well. But in relation to the municipality attacks I don't large number of casualties. I see larger ones at Jajce and I see larger ones in the corridor, and there are the occasional references to people having accidents. So that, from the casualty component, is what I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, we will take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Going to be time for a break. I have just one document more. After break.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I very quickly deal with the point that I was raising in respect of Mr. Sejmenovic just before Mr. Brown comes back. Would Your Honours have a look, please, on the screen at part of the transcript. This is cross-examination by Mr. Aleksic at transcript page 17504. Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What is the date? [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Ooh. 18th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we look, please, wait a minute. Maybe six actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, we need to go just a little further down the pace. Now this is the question by Mr. Aleksic. "Q. To avoid going through your.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Line number please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. 17505, line 16. Now, Your Honours. Can I just ask Your Honours to look at it rather than reading it out. But he says: "To avoid going through your extensive testimony in the Stakic case" - and then purports to summarize that testimony, ending up with: "Is that fair to say? " "A. In part." And then Mr. Aleksic moves to a completely different topic. Now that is a problem, of course, with a compound question like that and the fact that Mr. Aleksic or indeed Mr. Olmsted actually, to be fair to say, I suppose, didn't stand up and say that is an amazingly compound question and what do you mean by "in part". And that was it. The document that was never -- was never put to him. As Mr. Aleksic says there was extensive testimony and his summary, we would suggest, is inaccurate. And the fact remains, Your Honour, and that's my reason for caution over this document and I don't, as I say object to it being admitted as to the fact because it's part of the report, but it is not, we would suggest, based on that question and answer evidence, that 2400 men were under arms. Now to complete was actually asked, Mr. Olmsted in re-examination did actually ask something about it and we need go to page 17523 to 4. And: "You were asked a few questions regarding the expansion of the Kozarac TO and I want to see if we can clarify the time-line here." And he then asked about the meeting. "And then returning to Kozarac when the decision was made to expand the TO." Now because the document which should have been put at that stage to him was never put, Mr. Olmsted obviously was limited as to what he could deal with in -- in re-examination. But the answer there was, as Your Honours see: "That was the period when intensive activities were under way to turn the TO into a proper establishment. The establishment of the TO practically started the same day when we returned from the meeting to which the -- at which the ultimatum was issued. We didn't even manage to finish this list. There was no time, there was no opportunity to go visit somebody for a second time to ask for their consent. You could notice about the list that a certain number of people were said not to be at home. There was no time to go back the next day or the day after and see whether that particular person was at home." So, Your Honours, at no time was a suggestion put to him: Those lists show, Mr. Sejmenovic, don't they, that you mobilised 2400 men. If it is going to be asserted that as Mr. Krgovic said that these lists show nothing, show that 2400 men were under arms then certainly we would request that Mr. Sejmenovic be re-called and deal with these lists properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I respond to this? First of all, I showed this document to the expert so that he could confirm what he had already stated in his report. That was all. I only limited myself to what Mr. Brown said about the -- this document in his report. That's ail I need. I don't need anything more. As far as Mr. Sejmenovic is concerned, the Prosecution had a chance to deal with it if they wanted to. Mr. Sejmenovic, however, is not from Kozarac; he happened to attend a meeting there. And I think that because of that, he is not the person who could testify about that. He is just an MP who attended a meeting. When he was asked in Stakic about it he said that he didn't know anything about it, about the strength, about the manpower. And Mr. [indiscernible] told him, So you know nothing about it? And he confirmed it, and that's all. If Mr. Sejmenovic is to be called here to interpret a document which did he not draft and the process of mobilisation in which did he not take part, there's no point in that. I have nothing to add to what the expert said about this document. Mr. Olmsted or, rather, the Prosecution, was aware of this document and was aware of the report produced by the expert witness, Mr. Brown, or at least that's what I assume. So no good reason has been shown to re-call Mr. Sejmenovic to testify.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Two things, Your Honour. First, we were limited by what the adjudicated fact was that Mr. Sejmenovic was dealing with. Second, the document should have put to him because his name appears on it. And -- yes, that's the other thing. Thank you very much. I have been reminded, it's not on our 65 ter list. It was disclosed to the Defence. So that was our other limitation on it. But as I say, in order to base that suggestion that Mr. Krgovic wishes to make that there were 2400 people actually armed and active. That is what Sejmenovic should have been asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know that any useful --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I don't know that is there any further useful purpose to take this matter at this point. Regardless of what has passed between counsel so far today, I'm disinclined to anticipate what Mr. Krgovic may or may not do. I prefer to limit the effect of this document to -- as Mr. Krgovic has said, it is a document which is -- part of the footnote in the witness's report and it is for that purposes -- for that purpose alone, the purpose of continuity, I suppose that it was relied on. Now what may happen and what may happen as a consequence of what may happen, I would prefer to deal with when we reach that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I agree but that is not what Mr. Krgovic said. He said in terms, I'm relying on it to show that 2400 men were under arms as part of my case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say that. I said there was a list, listing 2400 people, of which some were mobilised and some were not. And that's exactly what Mr. Brown said in his report. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we leave it there for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: For the sake of the record, which didn't pick up the overlapping conversation, the completion of my observations that we leave it there for the time being. Thank you. We will -- this session, which will conclude at the usual time of 1.45, we will resume, the extended session, at 2.30 and finish at 4.00 at the latest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 1D04-9090; tab 29 in Stanisic binder. [In English] I have problem with e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Brown, this is the analysis of combat readiness of the 1st Krajina Corps for 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, when, in your report, you spoke about the activities of the 1st Krajina Corps, did you have an opportunity to consider this document while making your report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember if I have referenced this document. I'd have to check. Is it from the Krajina Corps collection?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know this is a document that was only recently disclosed to us. Of course, it would be necessary to include this document into your analysis in order to gain a full picture into the activities of the corps in 1992.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would check if I have referenced this or not. I'd like to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I haven't found it. That's precisely why I mention it. Maybe I missed it, but I haven't found it. Now, can we take look at the first page - that is, the next page - on the screen. I think you may have mentioned it in footnote 713, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's there. Yes, I think it's referenced in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you wrote about the tasks. So, now, let us take a look at the next page, where they talk about reports, activities and casualties. Can you see here that in Croatia -- now let me just check whether that's the correct page. It's also the next page in Serbian. That's page 3 in Serbian and - just a moment - I think it's the previous page in English. Can you see it at the very bottom. "In the course of combat activities in Slavonia, 378 troops from the corps were killed and 2.874 were wounded." And then it goes on. Page 16 in Serbian; 12 in English. And here it says: "Losses, amounting to 2953 troops killed and 13.324 wounded, had the most negative influence on morale." Mr. Brown, when we take into account the manpower of the corps itself, which was between 65 and 70.000 soldiers and officers, we can see here that about 20 per cent of the combatants of the 1st Krajina Corps were hors de combat. That is a significant loss, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's 20 per cent, sir. At least not -- not by my maths. But I don't doubt, that the corps, as I said before, took significant casualties. And in particular the large operations in the corridor and in Jajce and on the contact lines in the sort of Vlasic area, and presumably I know that there were reports, soldiers on the front line in the corridor were being shelled from over the river in Croatia. So I don't doubt that the corps took a lot of casualties. These casualties, when hes -- he may well be talking about including all the casualties he had in Western Slavonia as well. They took casualties there. So I don't doubt that they took casualties. And other corps in other areas took casualties. And this is, you know, maybe over a one-year period, if he is talking about Western Slavonia he is taking probably from November to all the way through to whenever this report was written, or the end of December 1992, potentially. I don't say that the corps didn't take casualties at all. It did. And, you know, probably in some units the casualties were high. But my point is that when I looked at the municipality attacks, and you discussed that before, I didn't see large numbers of casualties being taken there, but I make no bones that, in the whole period of the reporting period and especially in the corridor area where the fighting, was quite significant, that the corps took casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, that information concerning Slavonia was on the previous page and that is where this comes from. That is what I showed you. You're saying that Operation Corridor was when? In June? That's when there was a breakthrough, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a breakthrough in June. It was expanded through the summer and they had to maintain the front lines -- actually, they had to maintain the front lines for the whole of the war. So there was a significant deployment of forces there. And there were instances where Krajina Corps units were sent to other areas. I know -- whether it is exactly in this reporting period but I know that some elements of the Krajina Corps were sent to other fronts. So you know I don't -- as I say, I don't dispute that the corps took casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the corridor, do you know of the members of the 1st Krajina Corps having been sent somewhere in 1991? Because sometime in the Autumn that was the area of responsibility of the Eastern Bosnian Corps, where the police brigade was sent.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's a long time, but I remember some component of the 1st Krajina Corps, I believe, was sent either to the East Bosna Corps or the Drina Corps, a small component, and it went off to do some activity there. But my point is that the corps was active. It was active in 1992 and it was active during this period and it had been active in Western Slavonia. I don't dispute if this is what's written as the casualty figures that that's what the corps suffered and -- yeah, I -- that what's it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In relation to the total number, Mr. Brown, the total number of corps members, very simply, if when we add these two figures up, 13324 wounded, 2953 killed, it's about 16.000 soldiers in relation to the strength of the corps which, at the end of 1992, was about 65.000. That's about 20 per cent, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you were talking about people killed. But if you add the casualties up, it may well get there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Hors de combat. That's what I'm saying, so I'm including both the wounded and the killed. I understand that to be a military term. Mr. Brown, let's move on to page 46 of this document. There you're going to see the losses per month. You see -- I mean, it's the same page in English too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's just the list. It probably hasn't been translated for some reason. Because it is Attachment number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You see the wounded in the first column and in the last one, the killed persons, POG, poginolje [phoen] so look at January, February, March, April ment and then from May onwards, when the conflict started in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You see that the number is on the rise all the way up to December 1992?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it doesn't surprise me. But, again, I would say that, you know, the casualties are significant, become more significant, and the conflict generally begins to break out but in particular in the months of July, August -- June, July, August, and that's when the corridor operation is, and later on you have operations in Jajce. I mean, I'm going from the B/C/S version and if you tell me that the last column is killed at least that would say -- and I guess maybe the wounded column would mirror that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, as far as I can recall, that document of the 24th of June that was shown to you by Mr. Zecevic, I think, it says that Operation Corridor was over by that date. So these losses, in September, October, November, December, have to do with Operation Jajce. So from June all the way up to December there is an constant trend: Over 200 casualties per month, and over 1.000 wounded soldiers per month. My question was, when speaking of losses and the strength of the other side, I mean, this refers to the strength of the other side, how well equipped and armed the other side was. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it -- I can't say whether it is well or not. I mean, Operation Corridor, to answer your first part first, it was initiated in June, and they were successful within a number of weeks or days, I think, actually, in establishing a corridor link. But there were subsequent operations after that to expand the corridor all the way up to the river. The initial success of the corridor, in essence followed the road linking the East Bosna Corps and the Krajina Corps. But follow-on operations in July and August and actually continuing through most of the year related to expanding the corridor all the way up to the river. And then once they'd succeeded in that, there was the problem of Croatian forces over the river conducting operations or shelling and conducting -- so they presumably took some casualties there. Concurrently with that, they also had a problem in the Doboj area and in essence the front line between Central Bosnia and Doboj, and that continued through the period of -- of summer, late summer, and into the end. So, yes, the initial success of the Operation Corridor was in a matter of weeks in achieving the goal of getting the link but it continued to be a problem for the corps in terms of clearing out the area initially and holding on to the territory both from Croatia to the north ands in the Central Bosnia issue in the south. In Jajce, Jajce is a pretty difficult place. It's relatively mountainous. It is it -- it was probably quite a good - easier - place to defend and it was a struggle for the corps to take that territory and I'm assuming that a lot of the casualties, maybe some of the casualties that relate to the summer are a reflection of that. It's large gorges, it's quite mountainous and it -- it wasn't initially successful as Operation Corridor for example. Then once they succeeded with that there was always the lines of contacts with Central Bosnia which presumably by that time I make no bones there was a defensive component or an armed component on that line of contact and presumably the casualties figures reference that. I think I said that on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, are we not getting far away from the nature of the attack against individual villages and municipalities in this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Mr. Brown gave an extensive answer and I actually wanted to narrow it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Brown, if we look at this report as it is, you cannot infer who was killed during individual attacks at various locations mentioned in the indictment, and who were those who were killed in other locations that are not mentioned in the indictment specifically the locations you mentioned in your report, Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kljuc?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think you can infer or extract that from these general corps-wide figures. I do know or do remember of one document in late May, maybe in the first day or so of June, which is a combat report in which -- or it might be a summary report, in which they discuss the issue of territory of Kljuc being taken over, activities in Sanski Most and in particular referencing activities in Prijedor. They go on to say that the 343rd brigade was involved, and in a line there they say in combat action I think 8 -- 8 soldiers were killed and 24 wounded. It is not clear if he is specifically referring to Prijedor or whether he is referring to all the combat operations in those municipalities at the time. So that's one that I can remember, but I don't see that there were that many of that nature, and I think from these figures, they are general figures presumably being produced for a larger document and I don't think you can break it down as to where people were killed at what time and in which location.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, at any rate, the fact that the losses sustained by the corps were so big, shows that they were facing a very strong opponent. I mean, losses of 20 per cent in modern warfare, that is a lot. I don't know if you have that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I may dispute the percentage figures because I would have to go back and look at the size of the corps. I don't dispute that the corps was taking significant casualties at times. In some of the operations that they were asked to do, particularly Jajce, I think, and to a degree the corridor too, were maybe not easy operations and it wouldn't surprise me if casualties were occurring and maybe even significant casualties in individual units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As for Operation Corridor, I mean, all of these operations that took place from the summer onwards, that's all the area of responsibility of the Eastern Bosnia Corps because that is where the bottleneck was, as it were, and that's where the corridor had to be extended and this was the unit that fought the most in that area.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a joint operation between two corps. I don't know the exact details of the East Bosna Corps; it was a far smaller corps in terms of number. I think the most significant corps that was involved in that was the Krajina Corps, in terms -- certainly in terms of its size but it was a joint operation. Both corps were to link up from either end of the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Krgovic, just on this question, but the thing is but I'm getting slightly -- wondering where the 20 per cent comes from. Page 3 of the document that is he referring to says the corps is around 108.000 people and then it says losses amounting to 2953 killed. That makes 2.3 per cent by my reckoning, or by my working out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, with all the figures in the report we can all do the arithmetic ourselves and I don't think we need get hung up on these percentages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Brown -- or actually, Your Honour, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 2D137, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we're bringing your cross-examination to an end. As far as I understood things, basically in your paper, you dealt with the activities of the 1st Krajina Corps in this analysis of yours. All of these other parts, if I can put it that way, were things that you sort of added on in passing but basically you focussed on the 1st Krajina Corps, didn't you, or, rather the 5th Corps of the JNA, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, predominantly the archives of the 5th Corps and the 1st Krajina Corps, and it was to do with operations in the Krajina area. But clearly in looking at other documents or materials I saw, it may have a bearing on that but it's referencing the Krajina area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The 1st Krajina Corps, that is, and therefore, its scope is limited. It does not provide what the situation was throughout the Krajina, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were a number of municipalities which fell within -- in the Krajina area fell within the zone of the 2nd Krajina Corps, I believe. I think we mentioned Kljuc was one that transferred at some stage and I believe that some of the other municipalities, if they're Krajina areas in that general zone fell within the 2nd Krajina Corps, not the 1st Krajina Corps, and I didn't look at that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In essence, this analysis of yours should be entitled, The military situation in the area of responsibility of the 1st Krajina Corps, rather than in Bosanska Krajina, right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, it's what it is, not what it's called.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in his report, Mr. Brown says that he is speaking only of the 1st Krajina Corps and the title says Bosanska Krajina, so this is the zone of two corps, right? Bosanska Krajina was the area of responsibility of two corps whereas you analysed only the 1st Krajina Corps, right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Although there are references in the 1st Krajina Corps to units that were involved in taking over municipalities or conducting operations outside what became the Krajina Corps area. For example, the 6th Brigade was involved in taking -- or in -- combat operations of taking control of Bosanska Krupa. That later fell within the zone of the 2nd Krajina Corps. The 1st Krajina Corps was involved in part until there was a transfer of AOR in -- in Kljuc. There are references to Bosanski Novi in the report, even though it subsequently fell outside the zone of the 1st Krajina Corps, although elements of the 1st Krajina Corps units were involved at times in combat operations there. Some of the municipalities in the Jajce area fell within the 2nd Krajina Corps and there was a joint operation at certain stages. No, I didn't utilise, generally, documents from the 2nd Krajina Corps. I didn't have their archive. But I do reference, where appropriate, documents that took about municipalities that fall outwith the Krajina Corps. So I -- I hope that it's as exhaustive as it can be from the archive about many or most, I guess, of the Krajina municipalities. But it's another limitation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So you agree with me that the document of your analysis does not represent an exhaustive analysis of all developments in the Bosnian Krajina in 1992, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's even referenced in the first page or the introduction. It isn't an exhaustive analysis. I think it could be a lifetime's work, potentially, if it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, firstly, the report. I'm going to deal with Mr. Krgovic's -- a few matters of Mr. Krgovic's cross-examination after that and I think after the break deal with the larger themes that Mr. Zecevic raised with you. Firstly there was a suggestion which came from Mr. Zecevic that your impartiality in writing this report had been affected by the fact that you'd been requested to do that. When you were asked to produce this report, was that for two reasons, firstly, of course, General Talic was on trial?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, secondly, in connection with the idea of whether this was joint criminal enterprise or not, between the army, the military, and the civilian, political ...

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I was asked with that in mind particularly. I -- from what I remember, when I first arrived at the Tribunal, there was this archive that hadn't necessarily been looked at in this manner and I started to look at it as part of my job, discuss it with my manager and it was clear to me that the document collection was very valuable. So there was a suggestion that an analysis report should be written about what this material may say. I'm not -- I mean, clearly that there was at the time was -- I don't think General Talic was necessarily in trial at the time but maybe there was an indictment. I forget the timing exactly. But this issue of joint criminal enterprise I'm not sure was one that was set as an issue at the beginning. It was a very general request to look at this material to see what the Krajina Corps collection said and within the caveat of a time-frame and it was left up to me to decide what should be included in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, that was the -- going to be the next question? Were you ever told what to put in that report?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. I organised the material in a manner that I thought appropriate. I never was asked to include certain sections and I don't think I was even asked at the end to make any amendments. From what I remember, I think it was a case of this is my report here it is and typos and all that kind of stuff. I set the report, I set the -- the table of contents and I decide what went in it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think you've answered what was going to be my last question, is, were you ever asked to remove something of your report, because it did not fit with any theory that the Prosecution might be advancing?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all. And I wouldn't have done so if I didn't believe what was in the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. All right. I want to go back, because we've just been looking at it, to that last document which has just been made an exhibit, the 1st Krajina Corps's own analysis which I think you said would have gone to the Main Staff for inclusion of the overall analysis of the VRS; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'd imagine that's exactly the process that occurred. They wrote theirs, it went to the Main Staff, it was compiled by staff officers at the Main Staff and then subsequently disseminated out. As we discussed earlier.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we could have that document up on the screen -- that's coming up. Can we look, first of all, in the English at page 3, which I think ... it should be same in B/C/S, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: English, page 3, please. Yep. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just so we see there, because I don't think your attention was drawn to it, the third paragraph: "The command of the corps immediately began mobilisation and supplementary conscription so that now the corps is composed of 48 units, equivalent to regiments or brigades with a total of around 108.000 people." I'm told it's the next page in B/C/S. Then if we go to page 12 again. Oh, B/C/S ... page 12 as well. Yes, thanks. I'm not interested in the figures of the troops you have been shown that already. At the paragraph at the end of the page in English: "We achieved significant results in activities related to prisoner of war exchanges. Within the 1st Krajina Corps's zone over 9.200 prisoners were exchanged, of which 2.300 were military personnel from the former BiH [sic] plus the bodies ..." So should -- Mr. Brown should one read that as showing that the other effectively 6900 were not military?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would seem to appear so, I -- maybe this is also a reflection of some of the documents in Manjaca where it is clear that they believe that many people who are in there, don't deserve to be in and were not caught in combat zones or don't have uniforms or weapons. And maybe this is another reflection that a significant number of people that were held were not in fact categorised as military personnel but were presumably, to all intents and purposes civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then if we go -- there's a further part about that at the top of the next page in English, page 13. "Our commission was not confined to the 1st Krajina Corps's area of responsibility and worked for all endangered Serbs. Although many criticise the decision of the government of the RS to close down the Manjaca prisoner of war camp they are not sufficiently aware of the effects of the exchanges conducted by the commission of the 1st Krajina Corps." And I think we saw somewhere else, Mr. Brown, that it was shut down in November of the previous year?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it didn't actually completely close until December. I think the last prisoners left then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then still on this same report, can we go, please, and this is really referring to one of the themes raised by Mr. Zecevic in which I'm going to return in more detail. But could we go to page 21 in English, and page 26. Although we'll need to go to the next page in B/C/S for that, what I want. Yes. If we go to the next page it's the paragraph, the fourth paragraph there. "In cooperation with the SNB and the CSB in Banja Luka, successful operations were carried out to identify the ringleaders and cut short illegal military organising by Muslim and Croatian elements in the corps's area, the plan for which did not give us any great surprise." Now it has been put to you in the most positive terms by Mr. Zecevic that the army in the territory of the Bosanska Krajina, 1st Krajina Corps, at all stages was ordering the CSB - I don't think we've heard about the SNB --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this -- this is not correct interpretation of what I said. I was -- I was referring to the law and the resubordination of the units to the -- the -- the -- the police units to the military command in certain cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, this says this is talking specifically about operations which -- I better ask Mr. Brown.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown what do you read "operations, successful operations were carried out" to mean?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he is referring to all the references that seem to occur in the Krajina Corps documents about taking control of municipalities that we've discussed previously. And maybe is he also discussing wider operations in the corridors and the likes. But I think -- he's -- as I have said, in a number of cases the corps documents predominantly discuss cooperation with the police, not the Krajina Corps commanding them -- the police, or taking control of CSBs, SJBs. Most of the references I've seen relate to the issue of cooperation. It's also not just the military documents that say that. Some of the police documents I have seen reflect that too. And there were clearly mechanisms in which police could be placed under the control of the military or to be involved with the military, conduct joint operations with the military, but it seems that the mechanism for that was to reach some agreement at the corps and CSB level and maybe in areas, in particular, I think, in the corridor, there probably were instances where police units were placed under the command of military. But in relation to the vast bulk of municipality attacks or municipality operations that I see, the references are to cooperation, and I imagine that to be that there was a police task, there were military tasks, and together what they did was to control that territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think the cooperation component is fairly routinely actually referenced in the military documents that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just -- I think I might of help to Ms. Korner. The problem is again with the translation of the document, you see. Because the translation of the document says that the particular part says, "in that cooperation." But it refers to the previous -- previous -- previous paragraph of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. Really, Mr. Zecevic can't give evidence about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment, he can certainly read out what appears in the document and I'm willing to listen to the translation but he can't assert that it relates to the previous paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can read the whole paragraph. But I would need the whole -- the whole Serbian page. It says in the original: [Interpretation] "The focus of activity in the first half of 1992 was on the Western Slavonian theatre of war and directed toward agents' positions and the uncovering and stopping of all forms of subversive activity."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You haven't got your earphones on. The interpreter is quite some way behind you. Can you slow down slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "... and stopping all forms of subversive activity. An example being in the units by the Army of the Republic of Croatia. And the second half of the year, also toward the Muslim and Croatian military factor in the zone of the corps in the territory of the former BH." Now the second paragraph follows: "In this cooperation, with the SNB, CSB Banja Luka, activities were successfully carried out to identify the ringleaders and the prevention of the activity of illegal military organising of the Muslim and Croatian factor in the zone of the corps in -- in which respect, we haven't had substantial surprises -- we haven't been substantially surprised." Your Honours, to my mind, the meaning of what I've read out in Serbian differs significantly from the meaning of this inadequate translation that we have here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you are referring to the "in this cooperation"? Which is not reflected in the translation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is why I said it refers to the previous paragraph. Because it said "in this cooperation" and they were talking about the cooperation in the previous [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... thank you. It was just to clarify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see no reference to any earlier cooperation in that paragraph. But I don't want to waste time and I think it is a matter for argument and submission. But can we turn over the page, please, to page 22 in English, and I would have thought it is ... oh, it is, yep. It says: "The work of the security organs and the military police is closely connected with the organs and services of the CSB and the military prosecutor's office in the corps zone, and on this level, we have had a number of positive experiences and results." You were shown a number of documents I think many ever Mr. Zecevic which showed tension, as it were. From your overall reading and analysis of the documents, how would you see this as a summary of the activity between them, CSB and the corps.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I say in my report that the relationship at times wasn't seamless and that there were tensions. I don't doubt that was the case. But it doesn't seem to have been of such magnitude that the system collapsed and broke down and these -- both those organs were -- were unable to function and at each other's throats, despite these problems General Talic appeared to be saying, We have cooperated, we have a need to cooperate, and there's been positive results because of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That all's want to ask you about that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, if I may, could we have page 12 of this document on the screen, please. Mr. Brown, in the last paragraph 9.200 prisoners were exchanged of which 2.300 were military personnel from the former BH ..." It's the word "former, the former BH" that strikes me. Is this, in your opinion -- does this in your opinion make a difference between prisoners of war, military from the opposite side in general as opposed to civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he is making a difference here that a number of the people he is categorising as military personnel whether they've been captured in the zone of combat operations throughout the whole of 1992. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So you take it that this phrasing, this language, means every armed man taken prisoner in the combat zone? It's not a more restricted category, in your opinion. I was just wondering. I was a little bit puzzled by the language used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the way I read this is they've taken a large number of persons and a small section of them 2.300, they view as being military personnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, can we then deal with a couple of other matters raised by Mr. Krgovic today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At page 54, line 12, he asserted to the Judges that, in your report, you described the forces of the Muslims and Croats as unorganized and unarmed. And just let's get an accurate reflection of what you did say in your report, please. Paragraph 2.205. Did you describe them in that paragraph: "In relation to specific weaponry available to non-Serbs this often appeared limited, both in terms of numbers and compatibility."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Ms. Korner, and I believe that to be the case. I didn't see many examples, if any actually. I'm not talking about necessarily what was happening from Croatia, sometimes artillery was used over the river or from Central Bosnia, but in the municipalities, I very rarely saw if any reference to heavy weapons, and by that I mean artillery, large-calibre machine-guns. I -- I think the weaponry that they seemed to have was somewhat limited to small arms.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And at paragraph 2.209, you talk again about the limited weaponry, and then say: "Some general comments on the comparison between non-Serbs and the VRS should be noted. The non-Serb forces were in the position of having to organise a completely new structure at best on the remnants of the Bosnia and Herzegovina TO or local manpower. The Serb forces were part of a recognised and structured military and police formations. They had maintained control of large amounts of weaponry and TO weapons had been put under the control of the JNA and the VRS had inherited ..." Is that the view that you formed when you looked at such documents as were available to you on the defence force -- the -- the non-Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, I think I would stand by that analysis of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then finally, and perhaps that's probably I can deal with that before we break, it was a document, 1D151 was shown to you, on the 29th of April, the order, I think, by Mr. Doko about the JNA and it was put to you that they were attempting to prevent the JNA leaving Bosnia by ordering fire on them. And I think looking at what you said about this. Page 47, yes, and you answered, in relation to -- there was uncertainty in relation what the JNA was and there was a blockade of Banja Luka. Now, I want you to have a look, please, at a document that you reference, in fact, in your footnote 42. It's P551. No -- thank you. It's coming on. And it's an article from Glas newspaper and if we look at the bottom: "At today's extraordinary session of the Bosnian Krajina Assembly, the region's National Defence Council and the Banja Luka War Staff were authorised to declare a state of war?" Just a moment. Is there a -- can we look at the next page of the translation. It may be in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, Your Honour, I didn't check. Because it came up during cross, I didn't actually check the document. I just better look at the reference in the reports here is what I want. I forgot it was such a long document. Yes, it should begin: "An extraordinary session of the Banja Luka began ..." -- Sorry, can we go back to the first page, I'm so sorry. Actually it is in the first paragraph. If we could highlight that. They're talking about the -- the JNA's new status after the proclamation of the new Yugoslavia and that some units of the Banja Luka Corps on the move. "However, decisions were finally ... forbidding any movement, to any extent of JNA units and their resources and equipment from the territory of the Bosnian Krajina, that is, from the territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." So does it appear from what you've seen today, Mr. Brown, that both sides were anxious to stop the JNA from pulling out, for different reasons.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think both sides stress the issue of resources and equipment. Presumably because they wanted to control some of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have dealt with all the matters that Mr. Krgovic raised, and I will move to the other matters after the break. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.44 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're waiting can I just ask, it will give me some indication, are Your Honours intending to ask questions, and if so how long do you think Your Honours will need, so I don't get bogged down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In short, Ms. Korner, we still expect to the finish the witness well within the 90 minutes that we have set aside.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Brown, I now want to go back to some of the matters you were asked about by Mr. Zecevic. At page 1880 [sic] of the transcript, he was asking you about the dismissals in the 1st Krajina Corps, and he put it to that you because they came from, in inverted commas, a different ethnicity it was justified to dismiss them and what he put to you was as I say at page 18880: "Certain officers of the 1st Krajina Corps whilst they were discharging their duties did things that were absolutely in contravention of both of law and military ethnics. Under such circumstances you would agree with me that their removal would have been fully justified, wouldn't you?" And you said: "Well, from the documents that I have seen, I don't think the non-Serbs in the military were removed on the basis of contravention of law and military ethics." So I would like to you have a look at some of those documents, please. Could we have up exhibit -- oh, golly, P1295, I hope. Oh, yes, sorry, .18, just a moment. Yes, P1295.18. And I think you reference this document in your report, 9th of June, Colonel Vukelic, reporting on the meeting of the Crisis Staff of the -- the regional Crisis Staff, and said there: "It was stated that within the units of the 1st Krajina Corps, and the units of the air force, anti-aircraft, et cetera, there are 67 officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality. An ultimatum was issued requesting removal of these persons from vital command posts." And that's the document you had in mind, was it, when you gave that answer to Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think the Crisis Staff clearly were unhappy with this. They put pressure on the corps, the corps indicated that they were -- that they -- the demand was justified but that they had problems in essence trying to replace the officers that were to be purged, but they recommend, the corps, that is, that they accelerate this process of sending them back to the FRY for -- for processing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yep. All right. And let's in fact, as we'll see, the same day it appears that this was sent up to the Main Staff. Could you look now, please, at Exhibit P1747. Dated the same day as that memo or report from Colonel Vukelic, from the Main Staff, to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, referencing the document. And I'll just check. Actually, yes, it's that document itself which must have been sent up, because the reference is the same, 488-3: "Officers of Muslim or Croatian nationality must be sent on leave immediately."

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so they clearly decided to accept that recommendation and send them to the FRY for -- and I don't believe they came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Next topic then, please, that you were asked about -- that I want to re-examine about, rather, is this question of town commands. At page 18897, I think it is, no, that's where the questioning start. You were being questioned about document 1D365. And -- which was the general instructions about town commands which came out in 1991. And the question at page 18899: "You would allow for this possibility that this instruction may be linked with the document which we looked at a little while ago, P1783 which was order by the command of the 30th Partisan Division to mount the defence of Kljuc." Your reply was that, no, you wouldn't say it was linked. You said that: "I believe that in the Kljuc Crisis Staff minutes, a couple of days prior to this document, it was accepted and agreed that the defence command should be established." Could you have a look at Exhibit P448, please. And it's page 5 in the English and page 28 in the B/C/S. And may I just compliment you on your quite remarkable memory, Mr. Brown. It is a comment, because it was two days before. This is a meeting of the Crisis Staff on the 29th of May. At the session, the following was concluded under 2: "That a defence command should be set up than Major Bosko Lukic should be appointed its commander." Again, can I ask, was that what you were thinking of the?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Clearly they're getting briefings on the situation and dealing with some other issues and they've obviously had some conclusion at that meeting that a defence command should be established. I'm assuming there was some military representative there and there was an agreement and maybe what followed from that was the 30th Division's more detailed instruction about the defence command.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then at the very end of your cross-examination because you had been checking your report you brought to Mr. Zecevic's attention another document that dealt with this topic which was a -- a report by, again, Colonel Vukelic of the 17th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And could we have a look at that, please -- it's 65 ter -- this was not on our 65 ter list. But it has been brought -- Mr. Zecevic is asking questions about it and the witness reminded us of it and so I'm going to ask that it -- when I've looked at it with him be added to our 65 ter and admitted and marked. It's 10642; footnote 847 of the report. Actually, it's the assistant commander. Yes. I said it's Vukelic; it is, in fact, as we'll see, Vojinovic. It is dated 17th of June addressed to the Main Staff, the civilian defence sector. And can I just pause there because I said addressed. From all the documents that you looked at, do you understand that the person to whom the document is being sent is the person, the addressee, that appears under the date.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, it -- command of the 1st Krajina Corps dated -- 1KK reference number and its date and then underneath that is usually who it's going to. The other option is they don't have the addressee, in essence, above that title but have it right at the very end. But in this case this is going to the Main Staff and presumably the civilian defence sector means the staff officer, the equivalent staff officer at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we go to the second page in English, I think it's -- it's still on that [indiscernible] page in B/C/S. We see there: "The civilian affairs organs of the corps command, town commands, municipal councils, local communes and assistant commanders for civilian affairs -- for civilian and subordinated units have been engaged in creating conditions for the return of refugees, the organisation and the formation of the Territorial Defence staffs and units and the accommodation of UN forces." And again, is -- is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That -- I -- I think as a civilian affairs officer, he's presumably liaising with whichever body in all the areas of the corps deal with various civilian affairs matters and there seems to be a general introductory comment about what he is doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then the fourth paragraph again is he going -- I think it is Colonel Vojinovic is referring back again to a Crisis Staff meeting of the autonomous region. "It was decided that elected deputies should begin forming civilian governments in the municipalities of Donji Vakuf and Derventa with the help of the units of the 1st Krajina Corps in that area." Now you said as far as you could see these town commands applied in -- in areas where there was problems with civilian government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we have the Serbian version of the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, next page in -- I'm so sorry. It's there, isn't it, isn't the last paragraph on Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... all right. Although it may go over the page. I think it goes over the page as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. From the limited documents that I think I've seen, I would -- it would probably seem to be that town commands were rather related to areas where there was no civilian presence at all or no existing presence, or in areas where the corps had recently captured, if you like, and I think in this case it would appear there was a meeting at the ARK region in which these two areas were discussed and it was agreed that in order to form civilian governments there that they were requiring the assistance of the Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah. We can look at -- Oh, I'm sorry, Your Honour, can I ask that it formally be added to the 65 ter and then admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So admitted and subsequently -- so entered on the 65 ter list and then marked as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1798, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we just look at one further document on this topic, please, in fact specific to Donji Vakuf. That is 65 ter 899. You were shown some documents about that by Mr. Zecevic, about Donji Vakuf. This is to the Ministry of Interior -- sorry. From the Ministry of Interior the public security centre at Srbobran. Dated the 4th of October, 1993. Sorry. Yep. And addressed to somebody called Slobodan Jakovljevic. Sorry about the pronunciation. It's headed, "Chronological factual report on the setting up the a Serbian SJB public security station and police participation in the war." And it sets out the events in Donji Vakuf. And can we go to the second page, please, in English. And I think it's the second page in the B/C/S as well. Yep. The paragraph that begins in English: "The 30th of April." They talk about the bridge being destroyed, the mobilisation, and then the Serbian flag being raised. "Because of all this and because they would not lay down their arms, the Muslims moved out en masse and on the 10th of May, 1992 there were only around 2.000 Muslims left in the town. The police took over the task of disarming and apprehending the already known extremists. We were helped in this task by the Serbian army, which had already taken possession of all the strategic positions around the town. Of course, we were also assisted by the people. At that time, the only state or municipal institutions that were still operating were the police station and army command." Again, Mr. Brown, does that seem to go with what you were able to ascertain from the limited documents that you were able to see on town commands?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh yes, it seems that there isn't a functioning civilian organisation there and that the police and army are operating and that was the reason why later on they decided to establish one and seek assistance from the Krajina Corps and establish -- through the civilian affairs to establish some kind of municipal government.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that document be admitted and marked, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that this document had been bar tabled by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It has, Your Honour, but it doesn't matter. It's still easier to have it admitted and marked now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We've already stated our views on this document, and we objected.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case even more so do I ask that it now be -- I -- I am afraid I hadn't read the objections by the Defence but even more so do we ask that the document be marked and admitted. Mr. Krgovic can explain how any objection he raised still stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for the admissibility of this document, we've already presented our arguments when it was bar tabled. So I don't need to repeat my document -- my arguments and I think that the decision should be made in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I appreciate that you would have previously indicated the basis of your objection. But inasmuch as the present application overtakes the bar table motion, could you -- would be so kind as to remind us as the basis of which you objected, which may in fact have changed in the light of where we are now with the application.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as the objection is concerned, as far as Donji Vakuf documents are concerned, the Prosecution did not call any evidence in relation to Donji Vakuf, so none of these documents could have been checked, both in terms of the content or the correctness of these documents. No link was established through think witness and that is the essence of our objection in relation to Donji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we didn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, as for the Stanisic Defence, we have stated our views when the document was bar tabled. Right now, I cannot see this document properly. It hadn't really been notified and I would really have to look at the document in its entirety. I would have to read it in order to give the Trial Chamber my views on this now. We have already objected, so I really cannot recall at this point in time what our objection was exactly. There were several hundred bar table documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the document is inadmissible. It relates to matters which are outside the temporal scope of the indictment and the Prosecution failed to call any witnesses from Donji Vakuf. First, it's wrong to say it falls outside the temporal scope of this indictment because it talks about the events of 1992. Second, we didn't call any evidence on Donji Vakuf because we've got adjudicated facts but this document has always - never been removed or replaced - been on our 65 ter list. Third, the circumstances have changed because Mr. Zecevic opened the door to this by his cross-examination on town commands and Donji Vakuf specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, I really don't see any reference to town command to this -- in this document. Not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
