utterances.text: There is no reference to town commands but Mr. Brown's answer has been that where -- that where civilian government wasn't functioning properly that appears to have been one of the reasons for a town command to be there. This document supports what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think this is a submission. Because the document itself does not refer to town command, and if Ms. Korner wants to connect Mr. Brown's answer about the town commands to this document this is part of her submission at the later stage in the proceedings. But it has nothing to do with whatsoever with the -- with the town commands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And if I may add, Ms. Korner, you would forgive me for having thought from your previous answer that this clarified this -- what to us was this new problem of town commands but we now understand that it's a inference that you would be inviting the Chamber to draw.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you take that document, yes, it's an inference. But, Your Honour, as I say, the circumstances are now completely different, and I think it's as well, at least if nothing else, to remove one document from the bar table to deal with it now. As I say, part of the Defence objections are just wrong in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We will have the document marked for identification in the meantime to allow Mr. Zecevic to fully articulate such objections as he thinks he has. I think we have heard Mr. Krgovic's objection, but Mr. Zecevic, as I understand him, when he would have fully digested it, may have an objection beyond what he may or may not have said in the -- in the -- on the bar table application. So we would make a determination next week, but in the meantime we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, can I say that was Mr. Krgovic's -- that was a joint objection. He had Mr. Zecevic's objection. It was a joint -- I read out to you what both of them said. There was nothing further he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number, Your Honours is P1799, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Actually, while we're at that time, can we have the document back again, please. We might as well look at one other part of it. Just to show why it's relevant and clearly admissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The paragraph after the one I've just looked at talks about some of the -- no, sorry, the last paragraph on that page being: "On the 4th of June" -- I'm sorry: "3rd of June" - paragraph before that - "an operation was planned together with the VRS against a larger Muslim village. The police and" -- it explains what it is, "the police was giving the task the liberating the left bank of the river Vrbas and the VRS the right bank." Do you know anything about this operation, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't in detail. I would have to go back to some of the corps documents to see whether it is reported up and maybe who too took part. But it would seem to be a joint operation of which the police were dealing with one part and the military were dealing with another.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. Now, can we look at, please, the larger topics of the question of the military ordering the police on which Mr. Zecevic spent most of the time and the so-called status of the police if they were resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, just for a moment lost 1892.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it originally -- when you were asked to look at Exhibit P1787.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps we ought just to remind ourselves of that. If we can have that up again on the screen. Yep.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it was put to you that -- it was being tasked were being given to the police, and you said, at page 18923: I don't believe that" -- at tab 5.2. Can we have that up, please, it's page 3 in English and same in B/C/S? "There are specific tasks given to the police." If this was the infantry brigade commander giving orders to the police in Kotor Varos, what would you expect to see?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would expect to see a section similar to the sections throughout the report, 2nd Infantry Company, pioneer platoon, I would expect to see a subsection there with the police's units name and then giving very specific instructions in the way the rest of the subordinate formations are. I don't see that. Normally what happens in an order like this, all the components that are under your command are given a specific instruction and here he does that with the companies, the pioneer platoon, the security section and anybody else he believes he commands. If the police were subordinated to him I would expect to see a similar subsection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now can we look, please -- yes. You were asked. We can see -- not sure whether you were asked about directive 1, and I don't know why... yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm not quite clear I need to ask the witness about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we actually go to another document which you were definitely asked about. And that's Exhibit 1D -- actually, oh, sorry, 65 ter is 1D405. Now, this is the order securing the territory. And -- from the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 31st of July. And it was put to you, in terms, about this document that tasks were being given to the MUP forces and they're being given very explicit and clear tasks and that "there is no doubt that the MUP forces are subordinated to the army in this particular incidents. Wouldn't you agree?" And that's at page 18951 and you said, No, not agree with you, and indeed, you pointed to the fact that Talic couldn't order units which are not under his command. And I think you drew the Court's attention to the Posavina Brigade, which we can see at paragraph 5.6. Do you remember that, Mr. Brown?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now I want you to look, please, at -- at the end of this document at the distribution list, please, which you'll find at 18 in the English and 17, I think, in B/C/S. That does not contain, does it, the units -- it's not distributed to the units under the East Bosnia Corps command, is it?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No these are all 1st Krajina Corps units.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it does not appear that was distributed either or sent to the Banja Luka CSB or to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not on the list.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want you to look then, as it were, as a mirror document not unfortunately for the same time-period but around that time-period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is a document from the East Bosnia Corps, document, yep. 65 ter 10645. Your Honour, although it wasn't on our list it was disclosed as long ago as September 2006 to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do we see there that under 2: "The task of the East Bosnia Corps as follows. One part of the force is to defend the existent front lines, carry out or confirming(?), regrouping and then move on to the liberation of Modrica with energetic actions in coordination with the 1st Krajina Corps?" This obviously all to do with the corridor; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, maybe as I said before the East Bosna Corps were pushing one way, and the Krajina Corps were pushing the other in order to secure the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And three: "One part of the 1st Krajina Corps forces will lead the attack towards Modrica" - wherever it is - "with a task to, in joint action with East Bosnia Corps, break enemy forces ..." Now is that the East Bosnia Corps giving orders to the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's informing subordinate -- whoever's in the distribution list, presumable subordinate units of the corps that the Krajina Corps have a role in this operation and in fact they're leading the attack towards Modrica and there's going to be a joint operation with the East Bosna Corps to secure the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may that be again added to the 65 ter and marked and admitted. It arises purely from cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm not sure, Your Honours, that -- I haven't seen this document printed. Maybe it was announced that it would be used. But as far as I know only one document was announced that it was going to be used. And I haven't seen this document ever in my life. So I don't know whether it was disclosed to the -- to the Defence at all, and when. And I have -- yeah, I heard, Ms. Korner. I'm not disputing what you are saying. I just have to confirm that with my staff. And I would like to see the -- the whole document again before I would be able to give my opinion on the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, we are not quite certain of just how this document arises out of cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the part I just read, the suggestion was that General Talic is giving orders because the MUP are mentioned in that original order that he was asked about. Mr. Brown said, No, that's not right. And what's more, it's clearly not right because you can see that he is mentioning the East Bosnia Corps in the same terms as the MUP and he cannot give orders to the East Bosnia Corps. And what I'm trying to show is that you see exactly the same sort of thing in the East Bosnia Corps and it supports Mr. Brown's assertion that what we are looking at where the MUP are mentioned in these military documents in these terms is not a case where the -- General Talic is giving orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if -- if I may be of assistance. We do not dispute the fact that General Talic is not commanding the -- the units of 1st Krajina Corps -- East Bosnia Corps. But what I did, Your Honours, and what was the point of my cross-examination was that there is a higher authority which gives the -- the order for coordinated action and I have shown to the witness the directive by General Mladic to all the corps, to East Bosnian, 1st 2nd and Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. With all they got was the same -- some of them got the same focus, same target, and it was said in this directive in coordinated action you are to do -- to reach that -- that -- specific target. That is the whole point. I'm not -- I'm not suggesting at any time that it was the -- it was Talic that is giving the orders to the units which are not under his command. I'm just saying that he is - and I'm staying by that - he is giving the order to the MUP units because they are under his command and they are resubordinated to the -- to the army. That's the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We were going to have the document marked for identification, pending what you - but having regard to -- sorry. The -- having regard to your explanation, Ms. Korner, is it necessary to go any further with this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. It is all very well to say, of course he doesn't dispute. He knows that General Talic can't give orders to other brigade -- corps. But he -- it's the terms of the order and I see Judge Delvoie nodding -- he is saying, You look at that. He is ordering the MUP. No, says Mr. Brown, because it is exactly the same kind of order that he is giving. The terms are the same as in what he says about the East Bosnia Corps and you see the East Bosnia Corps using the same language when they can't -- And I think it is important and corroborative, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, by a majority, Judge Harhoff dissenting we'll have the document admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1800, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I know I show lots of body language and that's perhaps my civil judge's -- civil system background. But I would ask you not to comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, is quite right, and I do apologise. I should not have commented on that. Right, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we then continue, please, with what was put to you by Mr. Zecevic at page 18961. Yes, no I'm sorry. This, in fact, was a question by Judge Delvoie relating to the document that you were being shown which was at tab 52 in our bundle.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know, it would really help ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one comment while Ms. Korner is finding the document. I note that the document, the last document, P1800 was admitted, but I was informed and it was confirmed by my staff that it wasn't announced at all by the Office of the Prosecutor for re-direct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I haven't announced any documents for re-direct at all. I never do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We sent to you a document that we had not yet disclosed before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've got the wrong -- but in any event, if I can just stick to this. I have forgotten --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is it general practice or general rules about it? Shall we do that in the Defence case? I think based on guide-lines that you are obliged to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You were being asked by Judge Delvoie if -- whether what you were saying was that resubordination decisions as they can follow from the law and this is at page 18961 are made on the basis of agreements between the police and the military. And your answer was: "I would expect that they would be. I'm leaving out the rest of it. I would imagine there is a planning component and there is an agreement in relation to what the police will do and for how long they will be there for." And Judge Delvoie asked: "Agreed by whom?" And you said: "Agreed through the police chain and through the police command and agreed through the military chain." Could you have a look now at P163. Sorry, it's 1D -- I'm so sorry. I will eventually but I want 1D46, please, 15th of May. I'm sorry. It is actually out of kilter; it's my organisation, I'm afraid. But anyhow, if we can just have a quick look at that. Because it's under the general head of this. This is the 15th of May, Mico Stanisic order.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we go please to paragraph 7, second page in English and in B/C/S. "The use of the ministry units in coordinated action" -- Now I not sure what the word is because it's in Cyrillic, but no doubt Mr. Zecevic will tell me if it's the usual word.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- "with the armed forces of the Serbian Republic may be ordered by the minister of the interior, commander of the police detachment of the ministry, Sarajevo CSB, and chief of the CSB of the military for the territory under his jurisdiction. The commander of the police detachment and chiefs of CSB shall inform the ministry staff of any use of the units described in the preceding paragraph and whilst participating in combat operations the units of the ministry shall be subordinated to the command of the armed forces. However, the ministry units shall be under the direct command of certain ministry officials." Now there is a slightly different point which I wanted to come on to in a second but as I've dealt with that... It was put to you that effectively once there was resubordination the police who were there became military conscripts, as it were. How do you read this particular document?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it doesn't say that, or it doesn't say that to me. I think the first part of paragraph 7 would seem to indicate some agree of authorisation and some degree of agreement that where this is a requirement for police units in coordination with the army that that can occur but there has to be that agreement. So, agreement usually means meetings or discussions or some kind of prepatory discussion to allow that. In relation to your point, I think that is the case. I don't think -- if this is the instruction, if it was the case that police officers when they work in coordinated action with the military or are subordinate to the military, they become soldiers or conscripts, I would expect it to be very obvious in this document. I haven't read it all but I don't think it says, Point 8, when police officers are subordinated to the military, they become conscripts and are subjects to the law of the army and the service guidelines. If that was the case, I would expect such an important and critical order to be passed down clearly and it doesn't say that at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Very quickly, then, because we are running out of time. Could we now look at the document P163. This is a summary, Mr. Brown, of a MUP meeting held on the 20th of August in Trebinje. If we go -- which was attended by amongst others Mico Stanisic. If we go please to the fourth page in English and it is the fourth page also, I think, in ... no, sorry. Third page in B/C/S. Second paragraph. This is the chief of Trebinje CSB, Mr. Savic speaking he says: "Paramilitary groups were present in the area of the CSB but following the minister's order this problem was successfully resolved in cooperation" -- I imagine it's the same word, is it, in B/C/S, I think it's the second paragraph in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not. This is the cooperation. This is not the coordinated action.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: "In cooperation with the Army of the Serbian Republic."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we quickly move, please, to page 6 in English and page 4 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is actually just to note because it goes back to the point of town commands and you were asked for example about, I think, Bosanski Brod. "Mr. Bjelosevic, chief of Doboj CSB pointed out that most municipalities in the Doboj area are affected by war (Bosanski Brod is under occupation as are parts of Derventa and Tesanj)."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry, Ms. Korner, but we need the Serbian text. We're getting something completely different on the monitor.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Page 3, sorry, page 4. I thought I said page 4, but obviously not. Page 4 in B/C/S and it should be the second paragraph -- sorry, fourth, one, two, three -- fifth paragraph down. "Chief of the Doboj CSB, Mr. Bjelosevic pointed out that most municipalities in the Doboj region are affected by the war (Bosanski Brod under occupation, as are parts of Derventa and Tesanj), while the town of Doboj is constantly under artillery attack [sic]." Finally, this is the part I wanted to ask you about. Can we go to page 7 in English and 5 in B/C/S. "In the previous period all the police officers participated in combat activities at front lines confirmed by the number of those killed. There is also an increase in the requests by the Serbian Republic army commands for police employees to be sent to the front," et cetera. The word used is "request". Is that the word, Mr. Brown, you would have expected to see if, as Mr. Zecevic suggests this was the army able to order.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No it would seem to be another indication there was a process which the army and police had come to agreement that if they were required, they had to make a formal request and it had to be agreed, and that would seem to be there. And maybe the reference to the large number of policemen being involved in combat operations is because Doboj was on the front line. It wasn't like the municipalities in the interior or around Banja Luka; it was one of the municipalities that was really on the front line, as would seem to be indicated by the reference earlier in this document. Amongst others, because the military make many references to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, finally, on this topic, and I've only got two more very short documents, could you look at P613, please. This is 18th of September, 1992. It's addressed to the SJBs and the commander of the 1st and 2nd Krajina Corps, the minister of the interior for information and to the CSBs. "The number of requests by the lower commands of the army of the Republika Srpska ... to engage active-duty and reserve police forces in army formations on the lines of contact with enemy forces have increased lately," et cetera. "In connection with the above I wish to draw the attention of SJB chiefs to the following: In keeping with the agreement between the highest army representatives and those of the minister of the interior [sic] the Banja Luka CSB has ordered the restructuring ..." And, again, that was a document that you were asked about in connection with another paragraph, but does -- how does that fit in with your understanding?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe the police I guess are -- feel under pressure with the requests coming in but clearly there is this process, again, similar to the previous one, lower formations are asking for police support. Presumably, the police feel that they can't give that support all the time. Potentially, I don't know the details about the mop-up. Potentially, this restructuring was to try and keep the police down to the bare minimum that they feel acceptable and anybody spare was to be handed into the army, therefore alleviating their problem of having to use the police on the front line, but I -- I don't know the details of that individual issue. But it -- it -- it again seems to indicate problems that are viewed, meetings that are occurring and agreements trying to be arranged in relation to the function of the police, the use when they have to in front line combat operations and the needs of the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, finally, the assertion is made fairly and squarely, by Mr. Zecevic on page 18994: "I hope you will agree with me that when members of the police are resubordinated to the army they lose, first of all, their status of authorised officials and secondly, they gain the same rights and duties as any other military conscript." You were asked if you would agree with that and he said -- you asked, sorry, for the references, and Mr. Zecevic then said, "If I were to show you relevant legislation on which I base this particular claim, would it help?" You said, "Yes." Mr. Zecevic said he was going to prepare it but hasn't. But, in any event, if the police under the resubordination principle became military conscripts, or squaddies, or whatever the term is, would you expect then that they would be paid by the army?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Potentially, yes. If, to all intents and purposes, individuals ceased being a police officer and then to all intents and purposes become soldiers within the corps, I would probably expect them to be treated as any other soldier in the corps and paid.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If they were totally independent of the police chain of command and the police requisitioning and the like, would you expect requests being sent for the police to provide arms and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I would suspect that the military would be undertaking that whole logistic support.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can I just show you, please, one document. 10517 which goes back to this police brigade under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel Peulic. And this is to the MUP of the Republika Srpska Bijeljina. "Subject, request for the following: We ask you to provide the following ammunition for the needs of the police brigade of the CSB Banja Luka." And actually calls it the police brigade of the CSB, and it's dated 23rd of December. Again, if this was a completely -- these were army people under an army command, would you expect a request like that and addressed in those terms?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I would expect -- I would expect Colonel Peulic to go to logistic base in Banja Luka or through the staff to the logistics officer there, and I would have expected him -- potentially it might been easier for him to get through the logistics chain bearing in mind he was a commander in the corps and would presumably would have had to equip his own brigades in Skender Vakuf and Kotor Varos and presumably knew a logistic base commander in Banja Luka well. I would more have expected him to ask that through the military chain. If that -- if they were at all, to all intents and purposes soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, although it was part and parcel of a particular set of documents, it wasn't on our 65 ter list and I think the point is made without the necessity, Judge, you would be happy to hear, of making it an exhibit in this case. Your Honours, finally, and I see the time, as I just read out, Mr. Zecevic promised that he would give the -- Mr. Brown, and indeed myself, because I have made the request, the sections of the law which he says prove the assertions he's making. He has declined to do that. Your Honours, I, may I say, have got a whole tab of law documents which are all in the law library to demonstrate properly through a witness that his assertions, as such, are not borne out by anything we've seen, but as I say, we're always open to being shown the relevant documentation. But it seems to me that given the time and given the fact that Mr. Brown can only -- it is it effectively me just reading the documents, I will leave it. But I want to repeat the request that I made that Mr. Zecevic produce the regulations and the laws that he says enable him to make that assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Zecevic is reminded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's all I have for Mr. Brown in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I was just -- I'm not aware what is the status of this last document? I understand --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We do not oppose, because -- because the problem with this document, Your Honour, the document contains some other comments on itself, which -- which clearly indicate that -- that the -- that the explanation given by -- by this witness in -- in the -- in this re-direct right now is completely wrong. And, therefore, I -- now I have to ask that this document be admitted. Because the reference to this document and the comment by the expert is on the record. And the document clearly does not say that, and we can explain that in the meantime during the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm perfectly happy -- I didn't bring it up because I didn't want to start an argument - I'm perfectly happy to have it made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P1801.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That should be a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise, as Exhibit 1D418.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I should have formally asked -- I think there's a problem with the exhibit number. I don't think it has come out properly on the transcript. I should formally ask to move into evidence Mr. Brown's original report and his extra report on the Mladic diaries and we will provide the Trial Chamber with a list of the footnotes which are on our 65 ter list and which we would like to have admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, the 1D of the document is not recorded properly. I'm not sure what is the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number is 1D418, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Can we have exhibit number 1D410 on the screen, please. Mr. Brown, this is one of Colonel Lisica's orders. You see that.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do sir, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: To me, when it was discussed here, it looked as -- a case of resubordination, yet you seem to be very reluctant to qualify it as an example of resubordination order. So I wonder whether there's something I -- I'm missing. So I need your expert opinion why are you not calling this a straightforward example of a resubordination order. Or did I understand you -- did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't necessarily make myself clear. I don't know what the agreements could have been that resulted from this, but it would seem that Colonel Lisica is instructing the formation of a mixed battalion which includes a police component and this appointment as the battalion commander. And I am assuming that what is he doing is he is going to utilise or that his tactical group is going to utilise that. What I'm saying is I am not sure what may have preceded that allowing him the authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I do agree with that. But I was not referring to the agreement that leads to, in your opinion, a resubordination order; I was just referring to the order as such, regardless of how it came to be. And then do you then agree that this is a resubordination order?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would appear to have a mixed battalion that he can issue instructions to, so I am assuming it is under his authority, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then one other question. In normal circumstances, outside any context of war, it is misbehaviour for a police officer to abandon his post, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would very much agree with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. And he will be punished if he does so, whether it is criminal penalty or disciplinary, right? But, on the other hand, to abandon a combat post for a military is another kind of crime, right?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you happen to know what in RS was the penalty for that?

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I believe the guide-lines which we saw at some stage during the cross-examination, the guide-lines for criminal prosecution, make a list of -- of that. I'm not sure what the penalty was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But it would be much more severe, I suppose, than the penalty for a police officer leaving his post at a -- at a traffic light.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suspect so from a military perspective leaving your post is -- I mean, [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: In wartime [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... in wartime, at the front line, if you leave your post -- although you can leave your post in different guises. You can do the same thing being at a check-point and you leave to go back to your home. Or you could leave in a barracks, but in the front line we're talking about absenting yourself from the front line. That is a very severe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now my question is, when you remember the document in which General Talic reported to CSB, the 79 policemen that left their combat posts, and there was a discussion about, was this an order or a request to the police to -- to -- to initiate prosecution, and you took it as -- as such. But then my question is: What would General Talic expect the CSB to do then? Prosecute that, initiate prosecution as -- for the military crime? Not for the police misbehaviour, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: EWAN BROWN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only go, I think, by what the guide-lines say, and the guide-lines and service regulations apply only to military personnel and military personnel are defined as soldiers, cadets, active and reserve members of the army and it may well have been, irrespective of what General Talic would have liked to have done, felt under the military law he had not got the jurisdiction to do that and that he is passing that to the CSB for them. Now it may well have been that there was no quite equivalent code -- charge in the civil code or the regulations for the MUP. It may be that negligence or dereliction of duty or a more general crime could have been more -- but I don't see that -- that the -- the guide-lines apply directly and I think what General Talic is doing is leaving it to the CSB to come up with the appropriate disciplinary process or charge that falls within the CSB's remit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's all I ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, we thank you, Mr. Brown, for your evidence before the Tribunal. You are now released and we wish you a safe journey either back to your home or onward to your next assignment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I very much appreciate your time, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we take the adjournment to Monday morning, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, sorry, can I have a ruling on whether I can have the report, the second report and the Mladic notebooks admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thought we had so ruled. This is a question of the numbers that the registry must assign, in the usual manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I must have missed that Your Honour, completely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
